The Dragon's Envoy

The dragonlord's envoy stands before me in the great hall with Aegon's answer, and I make him give it before my lords. I offered Aegon Targaryen my daughter's hand and, as her dowry, the lands east of the Gods Eye between the Trident and the Blackwater, country the Storm Kings once held and Harren Hoare holds now. In return I asked for Dragonstone beside me when the time came to settle with Harren. There was sense in it. If Aegon wanted land, Harren had more than enough to lose, and I have never lacked the stomach to take it from him.

Aegon refuses the marriage. He has two wives already, both his sisters, and the heathen says he has no need of a third. Instead he offers his half-brother, Orys Waters, for Argella. The envoy calls him Aegon's companion and captain, as though command could put a father at a bastard's wedding or give him a name worth carving above a gate. Orys is baseborn, and Aegon proposes to put him in my daughter's bed.

That is not all. Aegon accepts the lands I named only as the beginning of the dowry. He also wants Massey's Hook and the Stormlander country running south from the Blackwater toward the Wendwater and the headwaters of the Mander. Those lands are mine already, held by men who have sworn before gods and men to Storm's End. I offered him Harren's hide, and the dragon has answered by reaching for mine.

There are men in this hall who would have the envoy thrown from the cliffs for less, and I do not blame them. Still, wrath is a poor reason to leave an enemy's meaning half heard. I will know the whole of Aegon's insolence before I decide what answer it deserves.
Guards. Take his hands. They are the only hands Aegon gets.
Say the whole of it. What else does the dragon offer?
Carry my refusal to Dragonstone. I have heard enough.
The Terms of the Bastard

I let the envoy finish. Orys Waters is to wed Argella, and the lands east of the Gods Eye that I first named will pass with the marriage if we take them from Harren. Aegon also demands Massey's Hook and the country between the Blackwater, the Wendwater, and the upper Mander. In return, Dragonstone joins me against Harren Hoare. Aegon's strength will be turned north, not south, and neither king is asked to swear to the other.

That last part saves the offer from the privy. There is no demand for homage in Aegon's letter, no tribute, and no claim upon Storm's End. He wants land, a marriage, and a common war, and for all his heathen ways he has at least remembered that he is writing to a crowned king rather than summoning some petty lord to his hall.

Orys remains the difficulty. Argella is my only heir, and the man she marries will stand closer to Storm's End than any outsider has a right to stand. Yet the Seven did not decree that a wife's house must vanish into her husband's merely because scribes find the custom convenient. If Orys enters this house through Argella, then he enters it on my terms. The child who succeeds her can bear the name Durrandon, inherit Durrandon blood through his mother, and sit the seat his mother's fathers held before Dragonstone was more than a smoking rock.

Aegon may have the lands he asked for and the marriage he proposed. I will have his strength against Harren, and Storm's End will remain in my blood and under my name. If that is not enough for him, then he never wanted an alliance at all. #bold Orys Waters may marry my daughter, but the heir to Storm's End will be a Durrandon.#!
He weds into my house or not at all. Send that word.
No. A thousand years of Durrandons do not end in this hall.
A Raven to Dragonstone

The raven leaves Storm's End before dusk. I write the answer myself, because the matter is simple enough to fit in one line and important enough that I will not have a maester polish the edge off it.

#italic Your brother is welcome. His sons will be Durrandons.#!

My lords have objections, and none of them are shy about giving voice to them. Some object to Orys's birth, some to the lands Aegon has demanded, and some to any compact with a man who beds his own sisters and calls it marriage. I have heard them all. The Seven may judge Aegon's soul when they please; I am concerned with Harren Hoare, three dragons, and whether House Durrandon still sits Storm's End when the fighting is done.

I have conceded land rather than fight Harren and Dragonstone together, but I have conceded neither my crown nor my house. If Aegon accepts the condition, Orys comes south as Argella's husband and the pact stands. If he refuses it, he may keep his bastard and learn what the stormlands cost by another road. #bold The terms are sent. Dragonstone may take them or choke on them.#!
We will have Aegon's answer soon enough.
The Dragon Answers

The answer from Dragonstone comes sooner than I expected, and Aegon accepts the condition without argument. Orys will come to Storm's End for the marriage, which will be made before my court and beneath the eyes of the Seven, and the children born to Argella will bear the Durrandon name and inherit through her.

The rest of the letter concerns the lands and the war. Massey's Hook and the country south of the Blackwater are to pass as agreed. When our banners move against Harren Hoare, Dragonstone will move with us. Aegon writes that he has no quarrel with a house that keeps faith with him and no wish to pull down an ancient line merely to prove that he can. Fine words from a man with three dragons, but I have heard worse terms from men with far less behind them.

I had expected haggling over the one condition I would not yield. Instead Aegon has accepted it at once, which means either that he understands the value of House Durrandon or that he is confident enough to let me keep my name while he takes what else he wants. I will discover which soon enough. #bold I asked for an ally against Harren. I have one, and I mean to see whether the dragon keeps faith as well as he writes it.#!
Open the gates to him. Storm's End fears no one bastard.
No. I will not marry my heir to Dragonstone after all.
A Wedding at Storm's End

They wed in the great hall beneath Durran's roof, before the Seven, the assembled storm lords, and enough witnesses that no man will later pretend he misunderstood the bargain. The septon names Argella Durrandon and Orys Waters before the Father and Mother, joins their hands, and calls upon the Seven to witness the vows. Aegon may make what excuses he pleases for wedding sister to brother on Dragonstone. In Storm's End, my daughter is wed according to the laws of gods and men.

Orys is not what some of my lords expected from a bastard of Dragonstone. He is broad, quiet, and careful with his courtesies. Men test him during the feast, as men will, and he gives none of them the quarrel they are looking for. I would almost prefer that he did, because a man's temper is easier to judge than his patience, but he repeats the terms of the marriage before the hall without hesitation. Argella's inheritance is hers, and the children who inherit through her will be Durrandons of Storm's End.

Argella has watched him closely since his arrival and has found more to say to him than she has said to me about the match. I will not call a handful of conversations affection, nor do I require it. Kings have married for poorer reasons than land, blood, and a useful sword, and many have done worse than a husband their daughter can bear to speak with. The marriage is lawful, the succession is settled, and the Seven have heard the vows. #bold Orys has entered House Durrandon. House Durrandon has not entered his.#!
Ours is the Fury, and no marriage changes that.
Pour the wine. The day has earned it.
The Storm Rides North

The marriage settled one half of the bargain. Harren Hoare is the other. His monstrous castle rises beside the Gods Eye, and the riverlands he rules lie between my kingdom and the lands I promised to Argella's marriage. If those lands are ever to change hands, Harren must first be torn out of them, and I have wanted that ironborn blackguard humbled since long before Aegon Targaryen learned to look west.

The storm lords gather and ride north by the old roads through the kingswood and toward the Blackwater. Orys rides with them, and Aegon's banners are already moving from Dragonstone. I have no intention of wasting good stormland men against Harrenhal's walls if dragonfire can answer stone more cheaply, but castles are not kingdoms. Harren has riverlords, crossings, granaries, ferries, and armies that must be held while the dragons earn the land I have paid for.

So the storm rides with the dragon against the ironborn. I would have preferred a son of proper birth at my daughter's side and a smaller price for the alliance, but the bargain has been sworn and I keep my oaths, whatever liberties Aegon takes with the laws of gods and men in his own bed. #bold Sound the muster. Harren has sat on stolen lands long enough.#!
The storm rides north. Harren stole from us first.
Send my lords. A king need not ride every road himself.
An Ally on My Border

Aegon Targaryen has come ashore at the mouth of the Blackwater, on the three hills where the fisherfolk beach their boats, and for the first time in my life a foreign host has landed within a few days' ride of my border without a stormlander reaching for a sword.

Massey's Hook is his. So is the country running south toward the Wendwater. I signed those lands away with my own hand and my own seal, which is a thing I have done for no man before, and there is no pretending they were taken from me. The lords who held them under Storm's End have new oaths to swear, and not one of them has sent me a complaint I would care to read aloud.

Riders came to these walls a year ago with word that dragons had been seen over the water, and men reached for their swords. Riders came again this morning with the same word, and it means the opposite. The beasts fly north once the muster is done. Harren Hoare spent forty years raising walls against an enemy worthy of them, and he will not wait much longer for one.

#bold The bargain is made. Now let the dragon prove he is worth what I paid for him.#!
The dragon is mine now. Harren will be the first to learn it.
The Price of Peace

The war has changed Westeros. Harren's grip on the riverlands is broken, and Aegon's ambitions have not ended with him. Reports from beyond my borders bring battles, bargains, submissions, and refusals, but none of them alters the agreement made here. The stormlands remain outside Aegon's rule, bound to him by marriage and treaty but not by oath, and I have no intention of allowing success elsewhere to make him forget the difference.

Aegon comes to Storm's End to speak of what follows. He confirms before I ask that Argella's children remain Durrandons and that the lands and rights already settled between us will stand. Then the heathen who once took care to write to me as one king to another asks for the one thing he left untouched.

He wants my crown. I am to surrender the kingship and remain Lord of Storm's End, with the stormlands, my vassals, my revenues, and my heirs left in my hands. I would rule the same country from the same seat, but beneath Aegon's crown instead of my own. Durran Godsgrief defied the gods themselves for this rock, and Aegon Targaryen now asks me to hand over what storms, ironmen, Andals, and Dornishmen all failed to take.

I know what war against his house would mean. I have seen the dragons at work, and only a fool mistakes knowing the strength of an enemy for fearing him. The question is whether I spend the lives of my lords and their sons to keep a circlet on my brow, or give Aegon his title and keep everything beneath it. #bold If I bend, it will be because I chose what House Durrandon could afford to lose, not because the heathen frightened me into it.#!
The crown is metal. Storm's End is stone, blood, and men.
Durran bent to no god. I will not bend to a heathen.
The Storm Bends, Unbroken

It is done in my own hall, before my own lords, because if I am to put down Durran's crown I will do it where every storm lord can see that no sword is at my throat. I place it in Aegon's hands myself. He receives it without triumph, sets it aside, and names me Lord of Storm's End, confirming the stormlands to me and my heirs beneath his crown.

Then my lords swear again. Yesterday their oaths ended with me. Today they pass through me to Aegon, but the men, castles, rents, judgments, and levies of the stormlands remain under the same hand. Argella is still my heir, and her children will still be Durrandons of Storm's End. Aegon has won a king's oath, not the right to unmake a thousand years of my house.

I was a king when the septon broke his fast this morning and I am not one now. I will not pretend that loss is nothing, nor will I grovel over it. Harren lost his lands, his line, and perhaps more besides. I have lost a crown and kept Storm's End, my daughter, my name, and every lord who mattered yesterday. Men may decide for themselves which bargain they would rather have made. #bold The crown is Aegon's. The storm remains Durrandon.#!
Ours is the Fury. King or lord, that much is mine.
The Envoy Rides Home Whole

I gave the envoy his answer before he had finished the offering of it, and I gave it standing, so that no man in the hall could mistake it for a thing still open to argument. Argella is not for sale to a bastard. Not for Harren's lands, not for Harren's head, and not for the friendship of a man who beds his own sisters and expects the Seven to look elsewhere.

Half my lords wanted him carried out in pieces. Fell said so plainly and Grandison said it louder. He went out through the gate on his own feet with his own hands, and that was not mercy. A king who cuts up heralds is a king no one troubles to send heralds to, and I have too many borders to spend that coin on one Valyrian's messenger. Aegon can have the refusal clean. He will not be able to tell it as the raving of an old man in a temper.

He will come south. I have expected it since the first raven flew to Dragonstone, and expecting it changes nothing. Ironborn, Andals, Dornishmen: every one of them came to this coast with better cause than a wedding refused, and every one of them went home short of men.

#bold He keeps his hands. He keeps his bastard. The rest we will settle in the field.#!
Send him home whole. The war comes either way.
The Whole of It, and No

I heard the whole of it. Every league of land, every clause, every courtesy. No homage asked, no tribute, no claim laid on Storm's End, and Dragonstone's strength turned north against Harren Hoare beside my own. I will not pretend it was a poor offer. It is better than any king in Westeros has been given by that family, and likely better than any will be.

It comes down to Argella all the same. She is my only child and the whole of my house after me, and Aegon proposes to settle her on a man with no name of his own and call the account balanced. A king may trade land. Land can be taken back, and I have taken some of it back twice in my life. What passes through a daughter passes once, and whatever is put in her bed sits in Durran's seat forever after.

So the answer is no, given whole and given knowing. No man will say afterward that I refused in anger without understanding what lay on the table. I understood it well enough. That is precisely why I would not have it.

#bold The dragon named a fair price. He asked for the one thing that was never for sale.#!
I have heard it all, and my answer stands.
The Raven Recalled

Eleven days I have had Aegon's letter, and eleven days I have read it and set it down and taken it up again. He granted the condition without a word of argument. Argella's children will be Durrandons, he writes, as though it cost him nothing. I named that condition because I was certain it would break the whole business, and a man does not surrender so easily the thing he means to keep.

Either he does not care whose name is cut above the gate so long as the gate is his, or he means to have that too and reckons it can wait a generation. I have sat across a table from men who conceded everything and took it all back before the ink dried. I have been one of them.

The envoy is long gone and there is nobody left in this hall to shout at but my own lords, who told me what they thought when the first raven flew. So a second raven goes tonight and it takes the offer back. Aegon will have been generous where all Westeros could see it and refused where all Westeros could see that, and the tale will be told that way in every hall from here to the Wall. And so it will be told. I would sooner be called changeable than be called the king who put a bastard's line in Durran's seat and thanked him for the favour.

#bold I asked a price I thought he would not pay. He paid it, and that is what decided me.#!
Send the raven. The offer is withdrawn.
The Goodson's War

Aegon has declared for my crown, and there is no dressing this as an invasion. His brother sat at my table two winters ago and swore before the Seven that his sons would carry my name. The men marching out of Storm's End marched beside those banners at the Gods Eye. Some of them buried friends from that host and will now go looking for the ones who lived.

He wants the circlet and nothing beside it. Not Storm's End, not the stormlands, not Argella's inheritance. He has asked for none of them and he will get none of them by asking. Only the crown of Durran Godsgrief, and only because a realm with two kings in it is not yet the realm he says he has.

Orys will come south. Aegon has sent Orys for the stormlands from the beginning and sees no reason to stop now. My own goodson against my own banners, and whatever grandsons the gods see fit to give me will hear about it from whichever side is left to do the telling.

#bold I kept every oath I swore to that house. I never swore them this one.#!
Call the banners. The crown was never his to ask for.
He is my daughter's husband. He will swear it.
Send him back to his brother.
Take him. He'll not command my men.
The Goodson's Oath

I have him brought into the great hall with every storm lord in Storm's End standing to watch it, because a thing done quietly is a thing that can be argued about later. Orys Waters is my daughter's husband, my grandsons will carry my name, and his brother's host is marching down my roads. Two of those three are worth something to me. I mean to find out which.

He does not make me ask twice. He goes down on one knee on the stones in front of the whole hall, and he says it plainly and without ornament: that he is sworn to Storm's End and to the house he married into, that Aegon released him of nothing when he sent him south, and that he will draw his sword for me against any man living. He does not say his brother's name. I notice that he does not, and I let it pass.

Argella watches from the dais and does not look at me once. She has more to lose here than either of us and she knows exactly what I would have done to him if he had hesitated. He did not hesitate. Whatever else the Seven made him, they did not make him a coward, and I have known a great many highborn men who were.

So he rides with us. Men will say I was a fool to allow it and those men are welcome to say so where I can hear them. I have taken oaths from better-born men who kept them worse.

#bold He knelt in my hall and swore before the Seven. Now let the dragon come and see what he bought with that bastard.#!
Rise, goodson. You ride on my right hand.
The Hook Comes Home

The terms are signed and I keep the crown. Aegon has not lost his realm and I will insult neither of us by claiming he has. He has lost a war he chose to begin, and he has paid for it in the only coin I wanted.

Massey's Hook is Durrandon ground again. So is the Wendwater forest and the woods along the Baywater, which means every holding south of that new town of his sends its levies to Storm's End now. The Storm Kings held all of it before a Targaryen ever crossed the water, and I have held it twice in one lifetime, which is more than most men manage with anything.

There is less satisfaction in it than I expected. Orys is still my goodson and Argella is still his wife, and there are storm lords in the ground who rode under the dragon's banners before they rode against them. A war won is a war won. It is not the same thing as never having needed one.

#bold He came for the crown of Durran Godsgrief and went home with less than he brought.#!
The Hook answers to Storm's End again.
The Price Paid Twice

The terms Aegon sets are the terms he set before a single man died. My crown for my lands. Storm's End, the stormlands, my lords, my revenues, and Argella after me, all of it kept and all of it held beneath his. Not one word has moved. He did not need to move it.

So I have bought with a war exactly what I was offered for nothing, and all I have to show for the difference is the certainty that I could not have won it. I told my lords I would not be frightened into kneeling, and I was not. I was beaten into it. The singers may find that prettier. I do not.

The worst of it is not Aegon. Aegon is a conqueror and conquerors take crowns, and there is no great shame in losing to a man who has taken six of them. The worst of it is that his brother sits at my table on feast days, wed to my daughter, and that the men who broke my host will be drinking in my hall before the year is out.

#bold I would not sell the crown. In the end I gave it away and paid for the privilege.#!
Take it, then. It cost me a war to learn its price.
The Muster of the Storm

So it is war. I have rejected Dragonstone and called my banners, and the storm lords have answered as storm lords should. Fell comes from Felwood, Errol from Haystack Hall, Buckler from Bronzegate, Grandison from Grandview, and Dondarrion down from Blackhaven with every marcher sword he can spare. Aegon may call himself whatever he pleases on his rock. South of the Blackwater, men still answer to Argilac Durrandon.

The rains have come early and hard. Roads that were firm a fortnight ago are mud from the Blackwater south, and every stream is running high. The Seven have sent me weather fit for a Storm King. A dragon can cross country that would stop an army, but Orys still needs wagons, fodder, dry bowstrings, and ground on which men can stand.

Orys is marching south with the greater part of Aegon's host, and Rhaenys Targaryen is with him on Meraxes. I have more men, better knowledge of the country, and lords defending their own fields. He has a dragon. I do not need to pretend that last advantage is small, but neither will I behave as though one beast has already conquered the stormlands. Where we meet will decide whether Orys learns that himself.
The kingswood. He will learn what my trees conceal.
The open field. No hedges, no tricks, no excuses.
The Rainwood. Orys can drown in it first.
Rain on the Kingswood

Fell, Buckler, and Errol struck the Targaryen van as it crossed the Wendwater. They came out of the trees at first light, killed men before Orys could bring the rest of his host into order, and withdrew before the weight of his army could close around them. By midday a great many of his men were dead or missing, and the storm lords had disappeared back into country they have hunted, ridden, and bled over since boyhood.

Rhaenys brought Meraxes up before midday, but low cloud, driving rain, and the tree cover kept her from finding the raiders in force. She burned stretches of woodland along the road and forced the storm lords farther back, but most had already scattered before the dragon reached them. I am told some of Orys's men cheered when she came overhead. Men cheer loudly when they need reminding that they are not afraid.

The ambush has cost Orys blood and time, and it has shown us how quickly Meraxes can punish a mistake. Good. I would rather know the beast's reach now than discover it with half my host trapped beneath her. #bold Orys has entered my country. He will pay for every road, ford, and stand of trees he takes from me.#!
Keep cutting. Give the bastard no peaceful mile.
Enough small fighting. Draw him toward a battle line.
The Wroth King

News of the fighting has travelled beyond the stormlands. Merchants and envoys bring questions about the Wendwater and about Meraxes being checked by the weather. The rest of Westeros can gossip. The only judgment that concerns me is inside my own camp, where men who once looked skyward at every shadow have now seen dragon men bleed like any others.

My lords have watched Orys lose men on roads he does not know. They have watched Meraxes forced low by rain and wind. Their confidence has returned, and I mean to use it before caution grows back into fear. A lord may be forgiven for respecting a dragon. He will not be forgiven for teaching his men to fear one before it appears.

Orys still has a disciplined host, and Rhaenys still has Meraxes. I know that as well as any trembling maester who can add one dragon to one army and declare the sum unbeatable. #bold We have bloodied them once. By the Warrior, I mean to do it again before they remember their courage.#!
Ride with the van. I will not shelter behind my lords.
Hold the line. Prudence is not fear.
Wings Pinned

The gale has settled over the coast and has not eased for three days. Meraxes remains on the ground above the Wendwater with her wings folded tight against the rain. My scouts have seen Rhaenys try to take her up twice, and both attempts ended almost as soon as they began. If the Seven mean to hand me a dragon chained by weather, I will not insult them by refusing the gift.

Without Meraxes in the air, Orys has to move as any other commander does. His host is smaller than mine, deep in country that answers to Storm's End, and forced onto roads the rain has reduced to mud. He may be Aegon's Hand, brother, bastard, or all three together. On the ground he is still a man leading men, and I have beaten better men than him.

The weather will not hold forever. When the wind drops, Rhaenys will rise again and every advantage changes with her. Until then the field belongs to soldiers, and no one south of the Blackwater has more right to it than I do. #bold While Meraxes is grounded, Orys will learn what became of every man who mistook the stormlands for easy country.#!
March. The Warrior has given us our hour.
Send scouts. I want to know whether men could reach her.
The Sky Turns Black

The wind eased before dawn, and Rhaenys wasted no time. Meraxes took the air low over the trees and found the storm lords who had been troubling Orys's march since the Wendwater. The rain had soaked the forest for days, but dragonfire burned through wet leaves, green branches, horses, and men alike. The Stranger took his due quickly once she found them.

Lord Errol is dead. Fell and Buckler brought back what they could of their commands, many without shields or horses, and every man among them reeks of smoke. They speak less of the men they lost than of the sound Meraxes made above the trees before the fire came down. I will not call them cravens for it. A craven runs before the danger arrives. These men stood until the sky itself burned them out.

I can replace horses. I cannot replace lords, and I will not keep feeding good men into woods that Meraxes can turn into a furnace merely to prove I possess courage. Anyone who mistakes prudence for fear may say so in my hearing. #bold The dragon is flying again. We change the war before she changes it for us.#!
Scatter the host. The beast can hunt shadows.
Hold together. Every bow we have will be waiting for her.
The Lords Waver

Three lords came to my tent tonight, and none of them came only for himself. Grandison spoke for the rest. Errol is dead, Fell has lost near half the men he took north, Buckler is short of horses, and every raven from the coast brings another account of villages emptying before the Targaryen advance. No man in the tent used the word fear. They are storm lords, and they have earned better than that from me.

Then Grandison told me Aegon's terms are being repeated openly through Orys's camp. Any storm lord who bends the knee keeps his lands, his castle, and his name. The heathen has learned enough of Westeros to know where to place the knife. He is not asking my lords to betray their homes. He is offering to spare those homes if they betray me.

Grandison did not ask leave to desert. He said that if I commanded him to remain, his house would remain and take whatever came with it. By the Seven, that is why the decision is mine rather than his. Their oaths give me the right to demand everything. A king who spends brave men merely because they are brave enough to obey him has mistaken pride for duty. #bold I will decide what loyalty to House Durrandon requires, and no dragonlord will decide it for me.#!
Hold them to their oaths. None leaves while I stand.
Cravens and oathbreakers. They can run home to their walls.
Bronzegate Broken

Bronzegate is taken, my army has been forced back across the Slayne, and I have perhaps eleven thousand men left of the twenty thousand who answered the first muster. The right gave way at the ford after Meraxes made repeated passes over it. Those men were not cravens. I saw horses burning beneath them and men trying to close ranks while their shields caught fire. The Warrior himself could ask no more of mortal men. Buckler died holding them together long enough for the rest to cross.

The road to Storm's End lies open behind me. I have sent Argella back with orders to prepare the castle and keep the garrison steady. She knows as well as I do that walls alone will not win this war while Meraxes can fly, but Storm's End has outlived every fool who thought stone was all that held it.

I still have an army, and Orys has not destroyed it. If I continue yielding ground, there will soon be no ground left between him and my daughter's inheritance. I can choose the next field, bring every man I have left onto it, and force this war to a decision before Meraxes burns the kingdom apart by pieces. I have retreated far enough for any man who ever means to call me craven. #bold The next ground I give Orys will be measured in blood, not miles.#!
Turn and fight. No man will call Argilac Durrandon craven.
Fall back to Storm's End. The walls have never failed us.
The Last Storm

Orys has taken the hills south of Bronzegate and dug his men into the high ground. In clear weather I would call it a strong position and let him grow hungry on it. The weather is anything but clear. Rain is driving across the field hard enough to blind a bowman, the slopes are turning to mud, and Meraxes is crouched on the hillside with Rhaenys beside her, unable to stay aloft in the gale. The gods have sent me a storm fit for the name Durrandon.

My host is larger, and the gale has taken away much of the advantage that brought Orys this far. It has not taken away the hill. We will have to climb for him, and every horse that loses its footing will open a gap for his spears. So be it. The Warrior does not promise dry ground, and neither do I.

I ride the line before we begin. Fell is there, Grandison is there, Dondarrion and Morrigen and what remains of Buckler's men are there. They have followed me through every retreat of this campaign and have not yet refused an order. I will not ask such men to spend another day wondering whether their king still has the courage to use them. #bold Sound the charge. If Orys wants the stormlands, he can take them from us here.#!
Drive at the center. Break him where he feels strongest.
Take the left slope. I will have his hill from under him.
Fury

The first charge died on the slope. The second reached the Targaryen line and was thrown back in the mud. On the third we broke into their center, and for a time there was no line at all, only stormland horse forcing uphill through rain while Orys's foot tried to close the gap. I have heard men call cavalry useless in mud. Those men have never ridden with mine.

Then Meraxes found room to breathe fire. She could not take the sky, but she did not need to. The front of my vanguard vanished behind flame, and horses that had carried knights through three charges tore free of their riders and ran. My own horse went down beneath me in the crush. By the time I got clear, my shield arm was numb and the battle had closed around us on foot. If the Stranger wants me, he will have to come into the mud for me.

The storm lords are still fighting. Every time Orys's men push into the breach, another knot of household knights meets them and the center holds a little longer. Somewhere above the rain a horn is sounding from the hill, and men ahead of me are moving aside for someone coming down through their ranks. I know who it is before I see him. #bold Good. I have had enough of killing men sent by Orys Waters. He may answer for his own war now.#!
I will meet him. A Storm King does not hide.
The Bastard Comes Down the Hill

Orys Waters stops a few paces from me in the mud and calls on me to yield. He gives me my titles, offers quarter to the men still fighting around us, and says that if I lay down my sword I will keep Storm's End, Argella will keep her inheritance, and the storm lords who submit with me will keep their lands. He speaks as though these things are already his to give back to me.

He is younger, unwounded, and armoured to the throat. I have lost my horse and shield, my left hand barely closes, and there are Targaryen men behind him on the hill. I grant him every advantage and not one right to command me. A man does not become my king because he stands on higher ground, and a bastard does not become generous by offering me my own castle.

#italic Yield, Your Grace.#!

Durrandons have been driven from fields before. We have been besieged, beaten, starved, and forced to buy peace, and still Storm's End bears our name. I will not be the first of my line to discover cowardice because Orys Waters asks politely enough. #bold If he wants the sword of the Storm King, he may come and take it.#!

Orys Waters stops a few paces from me and removes his helm before he speaks. Whatever else I think of the man, that much is properly done. He gives terms face to face while men are still dying around us, and he gives me every title that Aegon's camp has spent this war trying to take away.

He offers quarter to the storm lords if I yield. Storm's End remains with my house, Argella's inheritance is confirmed, and my vassals keep their lands. He even offers me a place at his own table after the war, which sounds like more than his heathen brother instructed him to promise and perhaps is. I can respect the courage it takes to make such an offer without pretending I am obliged to accept it.

#italic Yield, Your Grace. Please.#!

For a moment I understand why Aegon trusts him. Then I look past Orys at the men still fighting under my banner and at the crowned stag hanging wet above them. Courtesy deserves courtesy, not surrender. #bold I will answer him as one warrior answers another. If he wants my submission, he must win it with steel.#!
Give him his answer with steel.
Cut me a road out. They may say what they like of it.
The Storm King Stands

Orys Waters is dead in the mud at my feet, and the men around us know it before I do. He was stronger than I expected and quicker than a man his size had any right to be. Early in the fight he put his sword through my left shoulder, and after that I had no strength to waste. I gave ground, kept him turning in the mud, and waited until he committed too much weight to a cut he thought would end it. There is no shame in admitting the bastard was good. He is dead all the same.

I remember the opening more clearly than the stroke that followed. His footing went, my blade found him beneath the arm, and the man who had marched south to take Storm's End went to his knees before me. By the time my household knights reached us, the cry had spread through both lines and Orys's center was beginning to pull back from the hill. The Warrior may judge which of us fought better. The field has already given its judgment.

They get me onto another horse and bind the shoulder as best they can. Then I see Meraxes across the field, still grounded by the gale, with Rhaenys beside her and the remnants of Orys's host between us. I have killed Aegon's Hand. The gods have left one of his dragons sitting in the mud within sight of my banner. A cautious man would call that victory enough. #bold I have never been accused of being a cautious man. If Meraxes can be reached, I mean to reach her.#!
Forty horse with me. Let us see whether dragons bleed.
Sound the recall. I will not turn victory into vanity.
The Day the Storm Broke Them

I watched Meraxes on the hillside while my lords pulled the army back into order. For a time I wanted every horse that could still move sent across the field after her. Fell finally put a hand on my bridle, which very few men in Westeros would dare, and told me what I already knew: Orys was dead, his center was retreating, and my own men were too spent to survive another charge if the dragon turned on them.

So I sounded the recall. I do not like retreating from any living thing, least of all a wounded dragon, but there is a difference between courage and throwing away men who have already won my battle for me. Some court fool may call that caution craven if he wishes. He may come to Storm's End and explain it before the same lords who stood with me in the mud.

Meraxes still lives and Aegon still has wars to make, but Orys came south to break my kingdom and lies dead on the field he chose. My shoulder will not rise much above my chest, yet I am alive, my army is still mine, and Storm's End remains behind us. #bold The bastard came for my crown. The Stranger has him instead.#!
Bind the wound. I am not finished with Aegon yet.
Meraxes on the Ground

I take forty horse across the flooded field toward Meraxes. More men would slow us and draw attention sooner. Fewer would leave us no hope of reaching her through the guards gathering around Rhaenys. Some men will call this madness if any of them live long enough to hear of it. I have been called worse things by better men. The rain is so heavy that the dragon disappears between one heartbeat and the next, then returns larger each time the distance closes.

At close range there is nothing graceful about her. Meraxes fills the hillside with folded wing, pale scale, muscle, and the heat of her breath. Her head alone is larger than a warhorse's chest, and one eye follows us as we approach. I had expected size and fire. I had not expected the certainty that there was thought behind that eye, or that the beast would look at me as though I were the one who had trespassed.

Rhaenys is at the base of the neck, shouting commands in the Valyrian tongue and trying to get the dragon upright. Meraxes shifts her weight and the men around me lower their spears without being told. I commend my soul to the Seven, set the spear beneath my arm, and choose the narrow place where throat meets breast. #bold If the Warrior has carried me this far, he may watch what comes next.#!
Ride. Forty horse will learn whether a dragon can be killed.
As Aegon Willed It

Eleven men return to Storm's End from the forty who rode with my father, and the account they give agrees in the parts that matter. They reached Meraxes before the dragon could take flight. She rose onto her forelegs instead, and one sweep of a folded wing broke the left side of the charge before she ever opened her mouth.

My father passed the wing. Two men saw his spear strike at the base of the neck and saw the point go in. Then Rhaenys gained the saddle, Meraxes turned her head, and the fire took horse and rider together. None of the eleven saw him rise again.

He had removed his crown before the charge and given it to a squire. That is what has come back to me, along with his surviving men and the knowledge that the field is lost to us. #bold My father is dead. His crown is on my table, and Storm's End is mine to hold.#!
The gates stay shut.
The Dragon Falls

My spear went in at the base of Meraxes's throat where the scales narrowed against the neck. I felt the shaft drive deeper than I thought any spear could go, then the dragon twisted and nearly tore my arm from its socket. Men and horses vanished beneath her wing as she came around, but the wound kept pouring dark blood into the rain. So dragons bleed after all, and by the Seven there is a great deal of it.

I remember very little in order after that. Fell's nephew was taken by the wing beside me. Someone pulled Rhaenys clear when Meraxes lurched onto her side. The dragon tried twice to rise and could not. Each movement grew weaker until the great neck settled into the mud and did not lift again. Men who had spent the whole war fearing the sound of her wings stood around her in silence and watched the life go out of her.

Orys was already dead, and the sight of Meraxes falling finished what remained of his army. His men broke north toward the Blackwater, carrying Rhaenys with them. She was alive when they took her from the field, though badly hurt. I had neither the horses nor the strength left to pursue far, and I will not apologize for failing to chase beaten men after killing their commander and their dragon in the same field.

Meraxes lies where she fell, so large even in death that men lower their voices beside her. Aegon Targaryen may keep his sister-wives, his heathen customs, and whatever titles he has gathered elsewhere. One of the dragons with which he crossed the Blackwater is dead in my kingdom, and the crowned stag still flies above Storm's End. #bold The heathen will hear that plainly. The stormlands are not his.#!
Send the news. I want Aegon to hear who killed his dragon.
The Mud and the Blood

Orys Waters beat me in the mud before two armies, and there is no lie worth telling about it. He was younger, he was stronger, and he kept his feet at the end of a long day when I could not. When I went down his sword was already through me.

So I lie here in the mud and the guts and the blood, which is how it ends for a soldier, and I have never claimed to be anything else. Fifty years of war, and the ground was always waiting.

Aegon can have the field. He cannot have the last of it.

#bold I am Argilac Durrandon, and I will live forever in the songs.#!
So dies the last of the Storm Kings.
The Storm Queen

My father is dead, and before the day is out I have myself proclaimed Queen of the Stormlands from the walls of Storm's End. The garrison sees the crown on my head, the captains swear before the same men they command, and every gate is barred before nightfall.

Storm's End has withstood storms, sieges, and wars since Durran raised the seventh castle on this cliff. I have four hundred men within the walls, provisions enough to endure a long investment, and a fortress no ordinary army can take by assault. Across the bay, however, Rhaenys and Meraxes are with the force that killed my father, and no wall can make a dragon fight by the rules of an ordinary siege.

The crown will not stop Meraxes. It can keep the question clear. If Orys wants the stormlands, he must deal with the woman who inherited them, and my own men must decide whether they will hold Storm's End with me before the enemy decides it for them. #bold My father is gone. House Durrandon is not.#!
Bar the gates. Man the walls.
Send to Orys under a peace banner. Him, not his brother.
Send to [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] under a peace banner. No one else is left to treat with.
Bar the gates. My men will hold them.
You. Put that down and step away from the door.
[fab_ourfury_captain.GetFirstName], what are you doing?

My father is dead, and before the day is out I have myself proclaimed Queen of the Stormlands from the walls of Storm's End. The garrison sees the crown on my head, the captains swear before the same men they command, and every gate is barred before nightfall.

Orys Waters is dead as well. My father killed him in the mud in front of two armies, and so the bastard Aegon meant to seat in this castle will never see the inside of it. Whatever else my father spent, and he spent all of it, he bought that.

What is left across the bay is [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName], a dragon, and a host that has lost the man who was leading it. I have four hundred men, provisions enough for a long investment, and a fortress no ordinary army takes by assault. None of that is an argument against a dragon. It is only what I have.

#bold My father is gone, and so is the man they meant me for. House Durrandon is neither.#!
Four Hundred Men

[fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] has been camped beneath these walls long enough that the men have stopped using tents and started calling the place by a name. There has been no assault. Storm's End has never been taken by assault, and nobody down there is fool enough to want to be the first to try.

I have four hundred men. I had four hundred when I put my father's crown on my head and I have four hundred still, which sounds like steadiness until you count how many of them have wives and fields in the villages that host is feeding. Nobody has opened a gate. That is not the same thing as nobody thinking about it.

Meraxes is close enough that I can see her from the seaward wall, and I look for her every morning before I have decided to. Durran's descendants have been told all our lives that a wall standing a thousand years will stand another winter. None of them ever had to explain a wall to a dragon.

#bold The gates hold as long as I say they hold. I would dearly like to know how long that will be true.#!
The gates hold. He can sit in the mud.
The gates hold, and my captains hold with them.
So it is tonight, and it is my own men.
[fab_ourfury_captain.GetFirstName]. Not you as well.
Send to Orys. I will treat with him before they treat for me.
Send to [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName]. I will treat before my captains treat for me.

Storm's End has never been taken by assault, and nobody down there is fool enough to want to be the first to try.

Nobody has opened a gate. That is not the same thing as nobody thinking about it.

There is no dragon over the bay. That is the one thing in this siege that has gone as no one expected, and I have watched men on the walls look up at an empty sky and stand a little straighter for it. An empty sky does not feed four hundred men, but I will take what the Seven send.

#bold The gates hold as long as I say they hold. I would dearly like to know how long that will be true.#!
The Gates Open Without Me

They came for me at night, and I will give them that much credit, because it meant they were ashamed. Four of my own captains, men who swore to me in this hall with my father three days in the ground. They took my sword first and the crown second and neither of them looked at me while they did it.

They carried me to Orys Waters bound and stripped and gagged, and they made a present of me, the way a man makes a present of plate or a horse or the keys to a gate. I have thought a great deal since about which of those they had in mind. I have settled on the keys.

Orys had them whipped. He did not thank them, he did not pay them, and he had me cut loose and covered before he would hear one word from anyone in that tent. Whatever else may be true of the man, he knew exactly what had been done and he wanted no share in the doing of it.

#bold Storm's End was not taken. It was sold, by men who could not have told you what they were selling.#!

I sent to [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] under a peace banner and I walked out of my own gate to meet them, which is more than my father would have done and more than half my captains expected. There was no rope and nobody carried me. Whatever gets written about this afterward, that part belongs to me.

The terms are what they were always going to be. Storm's End, the stormlands, and the crown of Durran Godsgrief, all of it into Targaryen hands. Walking out standing bought me nothing at the table. It bought me walking out standing.

My captains are relieved and working hard not to show it, and I have decided not to hold that against them. Four hundred men against a host and a dragon was never a wall. It was a number I said out loud to see whether saying it would make it so.

#bold I gave it away. That is not the same as having it taken, and I intend to be the one who remembers the difference.#!

It is finished, and it finished in the field rather than at these gates, which is the only mercy anywhere in it. The stormlands are spent. There are no musters left to call, no lords left with men to send, and no road in this kingdom the Targaryens have not walked down at their leisure.

I held Storm's End. That is the entire account of what I can say for myself. The walls never opened, the garrison never broke, and none of it mattered, because a kingdom is not a castle, and I ran out of the one while I was busy keeping the other.

Aegon's terms come south with [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] and they are not cruel. They were never going to need to be. A man does not have to be cruel to a woman who has nothing left in her hands to take.

#bold I kept the gate and lost the kingdom. My father would have understood that arithmetic and hated it exactly as much as I do.#!
So it ends. Let me hear the terms.

Aegon's terms arrive without the man who was meant to bring them. My father saw to that much. It has made no difference to a single line of them and I never thought it would, but I find I am glad of it anyway, and I have stopped apologising to myself for being glad.

#bold I kept the gate and lost the kingdom. My father would have understood that arithmetic and hated it exactly as much as I do.#!
A Cloak, and a Name Not Mine

Orys Waters is to have Storm's End, and me along with it. Aegon has settled the matter the way he settles everything now, which is briefly and in writing, and there is nobody left standing in Westeros in a position to tell him otherwise.

He is not the creature my father described. My father made him out to be a stain, a bastard offered as an insult, and answered him with a box. I have watched the man for a fortnight and he is quiet, careful, unhandsome, and visibly uncomfortable with having won. That is worse in its way. It would be far easier if he were what I was promised.

He asked me rather than told me, which nothing required of him, and which I noticed. The answer is the same either way and we both know it. But he asked, and I will remember that he asked, and one day the singers will want to know which of those two things was the marriage.

#bold I am the last of Durran's line and the first of whatever this is. Ours is the fury still. It will simply fly under a different beast.#!

He put his own cloak on me before he asked me anything at all, and he did it himself, and he did it standing in front of the men who had brought me. That is the first thing I will say about Orys Waters and I have decided it is the thing I will keep saying, because the rest of that night belongs to me and I do not intend to hand it to singers.

He is to have Storm's End by Aegon's word, and me with it. I could tell you I was given no choice, and it would be true, and it would also be the smaller half of the truth. He asked. He asked after everything that had already been done to me, when not one man alive would have made him, and he waited for an answer he had no need of.

My father would have refused him. My father did refuse him, with a box, and that box is most of the reason I am standing in another man's cloak watching my house end behind me. I have thought about that a great deal and I am not sure I have finished.

#bold He covered me when my own men would not. It is a thin thing to build a marriage on. It is more than my father left me.#!

Orys Waters is dead, killed by my father in the mud in front of two armies, and the marriage Aegon designed for me died in the same place. There is no bastard left to hand me to and no cloak coming for my shoulders.

Aegon's terms stand regardless. The stormlands are his, the crown of Durran Godsgrief is his, and I hold Storm's End at his pleasure rather than by any right of my blood. What he has not done is find me another husband, and I have no intention of reminding him that the thought is available to him.

So I am the Durrandon who kept the seat and lost everything above it. Unmarried, unpromised, and for the moment unspoken for. My father would call that a poor bargain. My father is also dead, and the last thing he did on this earth was make certain the man meant to have me never would.

#bold He is gone, and Orys is gone, and I am still here. That will have to serve for now.#!
Give me the cloak. I know what it costs.
Then I remain Durrandon, whatever else is lost.
The Knee and the Crown

It is finished, and I am alive to see the terms written. Aegon's answer comes after Orys's victory, formal and almost painfully restrained. He demands my crown and my oath, but he does not demand Storm's End, Argella's inheritance, or the destruction of my house. The groom holding the feeding cart is not my groom. I know it the way a swordsman knows things, in the hands and not the head - he moves wrong, he watches wrong, and when I turn he is already inside the reach of any shout for help, a curved Dornish knife sliding out of his sleeve.

Valyrian steel is out of the scabbard before his knife clears the sleeve. He is quick. The blade is quicker. The Road to Maidenpool

Our first progress has borne us at last to Maidenpool, where every gate is hung with flowers and every bell rings for the coming of the King and Queen. Alysanne receives their welcome with one hand resting upon the small swell beneath her gown. If the gods are good, our first child will be born before another year has turned.

Even the wisest maester cannot make Alysanne scorn so gentle a hope. She laughs when I name it a tale for washerwomen and tells me that kings would be wiser if they listened to washerwomen from time to time.

Only women may enter the bathhouse. Ser Joffrey Doggett and Ser Gyles Morrigen must keep their watch beyond the doors, while Alysanne goes within with her ladies and the holy sisters who tend the pool.

Daggers Beneath White Robes

Prudence Celtigar was stabbed through the shoulder. Septa Edyth bears a red ruin across her cheek. They held the women off until Doggett and Morrigen broke down the barred door with swords in hand.

Two of the would-be killers died upon the wet stones. The third lives in Lord Mooton's dungeons, though she has more broken teeth than whole ones. Alysanne is untouched, and the maester swears the child within her yet lives, but my queen cannot cease staring at Rosamund's blood upon her gown.

She came seeking the Maiden's blessing. She found murder in a holy habit.

#bold Whoever sent those knives meant to kill my wife, my unborn child, and the peace we have labored to make. #!

The Guilty and the Innocent

Rosamund Ball lingered three days before the wound in her belly claimed her. Alysanne sat beside her until the end.

The surviving murderess has named six others in Maidenpool who shared her purpose. Lord Mooton would put every one of them to death, and cast all the holy sisters from Jonquil's Pool besides. He fears that any white robe may hide another knife.

Alysanne will not have it. 'Hang the guilty if their guilt is proved,' she tells us, her cheek pale beneath the stain of sleepless nights. 'But I will not answer Rosamund's courage by visiting vengeance upon women who had no part in her death. The robe did not wield the dagger. A woman did.'

There are lords who will name her mercy weakness. They were not in the blood-slick pool, nor did they watch three loyal women place their bodies before their queen.

#bold Justice must know one face from another, else it is only slaughter dressed in a king's colors. #!

A Shadow for the Queen

#bold Henceforth, the Queen shall cast a shadow armed with steel. #!

A Prince Too Soon

Our son has come before his hour.

The midwife lifts him in hands that seem too large for so small a child. His skin is red and thin, his limbs scarcely thicker than my fingers. For one terrible moment the chamber is silent. Then he draws a ragged breath and gives a cry so faint I must bend close to hear it.

Alysanne names him Aegon. The name of the Conqueror should belong to a strong prince, yet my son can scarcely close his hand about mine. The maesters wrap him in warmed wool and speak softly among themselves. Not one will promise us the dawn.

For three days the world has narrowed to a cradle.

Aegon's breathing comes shallow and uneven. Each pause lasts long enough for Alysanne to seize my hand; each little gasp releases it again. Grand Maester Benifer has tried warm goat's milk, steam, prayers, and every cordial known at the Citadel. At last he can do no more than stand beside us and count the breaths.

Beyond these walls, lords await word of an heir. Bells hang silent over the city. The Iron Throne may command seven kingdoms, yet all my kingly power cannot purchase one stronger beat of this tiny heart.

Night gathers at the windows. Aegon opens his eyes, dark and unfocused, and makes the smallest sound.

#bold Whether it is farewell or defiance, only the gods can know. #!

The Cradle Falls Silent

The maester waits, listens, and lowers his head. Alysanne gathers our son into her arms before any hand can cover him. He lived three days. Long enough to have a name, long enough to be loved, long enough for every hope we had laid upon him to become a grief with weight and shape.

They will call him Prince Aegon in the annals. My firstborn son. Heir to the Iron Throne for three brief days. A line of ink between a birth and a burial. No quill will write how warm his hand felt curled about the tip of my finger, or how fiercely his mother begged him to remain.

The Faith and the Marriage

The wedding is done, twice over, and yet the matter is not settled. The Faith of the Seven still names a brother wedding his sister an abomination; the Seven-Pointed Star, holy writ born in Andalos of old, denounces incest in the plainest words. Septons mutter it in their septs; the pious lords grumble; and I have not forgotten that it was such muttering that raised the Faith Militant against my father and my uncle, and drowned the realm in blood.

I will not leave this wound to fester. The Seven must be made to accept my marriage - but how? With patience and honeyed words, as befits a Conciliator? Or with fire, as befits a dragon?

I choose the path of my grandsire, not my uncle. I send forth seven of the wisest and most eloquent voices of the Faith - septons and septas both, among them the fierce old Septon Alfyn and clever Elinor Costayne - to preach the #bold Doctrine of Exceptionalism#! throughout the realm. Barefoot and alone they go, from village to village, town to town, telling the smallfolk of my wisdom and Alysanne's kindness.

Their teaching is simple: that the Targaryens, alone in all the world to ride dragons since the Doom of Valyria, sprang not from Andalos but from the Freehold, where different laws held sway and brother wed sister as the gods had made them - and that such blood is not to be judged by the laws of common men.

I will not burn them as my uncle would have. Instead I demand the oldest and most sacred of the Faith's own judgments: a #bold Trial of Seven#!. Seven champions shall fight for the Crown, and seven for the Faith, and the gods themselves will declare, through blood and steel, who is righteous.

The High Septon is too frail to lift a sword, so the Faith turns to its mightiest son: the #bold Lord of Oldtown#! himself shall champion the Seven, and the knights of the Hightower shall fill out his seven. And I shall fight in my own name - for the gods' verdict is not a thing a king may delegate. Each of us must now gather our champions, the finest swords who will stand with us in the yard before the Starry Sept.

If my seven prevail, then the gods have spoken: the Doctrine of Exceptionalism is proven true, and the Faith must bow to the verdict of its own holy trial. But if we fall, then I am judged a sinner before gods and men - and there is no appeal from such a judgment, nor will I survive it. The septons pray. The gods are watching.

#bold For the dragon, and for the truth. The champions will be gathered. #!
Seven for the dragon. Let the gods decide.
The Gods Have Judged

The last of my champions falls in the bloodied mud before the sept, and the septons raise their voices to the heavens in triumph. The gods have spoken - and their verdict is against me. I staked my marriage on their judgment before ten thousand witnesses, and there is no appeal from a Trial of Seven: to defy it now would be to hand the Faith Militant half my realm.

So the price is paid, and it is crueler than any sword. The High Septon declares my marriage to Alysanne dissolved in the eyes of gods and men, sinful and void from its first hour - and any children born of it are named abominations, unfit to ever sit the Iron Throne. And for Alysanne herself, the Faith claims its most terrible mercy: the grey robes of the #bold Silent Sisters#!, that she might atone for our sin in service to the Stranger, wordless until her dying day.

The sisters come for her at dusk. She does not weep where they can see her; that mercy she leaves for me alone. At the door she turns - and says nothing, for she has already begun her silence. But her eyes say what her tongue may never speak again: #italic it was never sin.#!

#bold I have lost her - to the gods who judged us, and the silence they demand. #!

The Gods Have Spoken

It is over. The last of the Faith's champions lies broken in the red mud before the Starry Sept, and a terrible hush falls over Oldtown. Seven fought for the Seven, and seven fought for the dragon - and the gods have rendered their verdict in blood and steel, as the Faith's own holiest law demands.

The septons stare at the carnage, ashen-faced. There is no appeal from a Trial of Seven; the judgment is holy, and final, and it is #bold mine#!. The Doctrine of Exceptionalism is no longer the plea of a king - it is the proven will of the gods, declared before ten thousand witnesses in the shadow of the Faith's own great sept.

The Most Devout may write it into their holy books, for the gods themselves have written it first, in blood.

#bold The gods are with the dragon. The Faith will bow. #!
The verdict is holy, and final. Proclaim the doctrine.
The Doctrine Written in Blood

Beneath the crystal dome of the Starry Sept, the High Septon lifts his voice before the assembled Most Devout and proclaims the Doctrine of Exceptionalism an official tenet of the Faith of the Seven. His voice does not waver, though every soul beneath the dome knows why he speaks: the Faith called upon the gods to judge the dragon, and the gods answered - for the dragon.

I did not burn them, as my uncle would have. I did not beg them, as they expected. I gave the Seven their own holiest trial and let their own gods speak - and now no septon may name my marriage sin, nor my children abominations, without calling the gods themselves liars. The verdict was written in blood before ten thousand witnesses, and it shall be written in the holy books for all the ages to come.

#bold The gods have judged, and the Faith must bow. The dragon and the Seven are reconciled - on the dragon's terms. #!

It ends not with blood, but with silence. The appointed day comes, and the Crown's seven stand armed and ready in the yard before the Starry Sept - and across from them, no one. The Faith, for all its thundering, could not find seven champions willing to stake their lives on its accusation. By the Faith's own holiest law, an accusation that cannot be championed is no accusation at all: the gods find for the accused.

The High Septon has no choice. Beneath the crystal dome, before the assembled Most Devout, he proclaims the Doctrine of Exceptionalism a tenet of the Faith of the Seven. No septon may now name my marriage sin, nor my children abominations - for when the gods were asked to judge the dragon, not one man of the Faith dared carry their sword.

#bold The Seven were called to battle, and none came. The doctrine stands, now and forever. #!
So it is written - in blood, and for all time.
The Faith of Old Valyria

Enough of this. Why should the blood of Old Valyria - who ride dragons, who rule the greatest realm the world has known - bow and scrape before the pale gods of the Andals, who came crawling to Westeros long after my forefathers ruled the skies?

The dragonlords of the Freehold worshipped the fourteen flames and the fire made flesh, and asked no septon's leave to wed as they pleased. So shall we. I proclaim before the court that House Targaryen forsakes the Faith of the Seven and returns to the old gods of Valyria. The septons may wail and the smallfolk gape. We are dragons; we shall make our own gods, as we always have.

#bold We are the blood of the dragon. We will worship as Valyria did. #!
Forsake the Seven. We return to the fires of Valyria.
The Realm Rises

The ravens fly, and every one carries the same word: war. The Lord of the Reach - in whose lands the Starry Sept lies in ashes and whose smallfolk sifted the bones of the High Septon from the ruin - has declared for the Faith, and the realm rises with him. The Riverlands. The Vale. The Westerlands. And the North - the Starks keep the old gods and care nothing for the Seven, but the burning of holy men alive in their own temple is a crime no honourable northman will suffer: they march not for the Faith, but against me.

Only the ironborn sit apart, praying to their drowned god and caring nothing for burned septs. The Crownlands stand by their king, and the Stormlands, who remember whose sword set me on this throne. Two kingdoms against five, and every sept in Westeros preaching holy war against the dragon who burned the gods' own house. My uncle faced the Faith Militant; I have made the whole realm my Faith Militant.

So be it. They wanted a monster on the Iron Throne. They will come and find one.

Fire and blood, then. They will find me waiting.

It is finished. Against five kingdoms and every sept in Westeros, the dragon has won. The hosts of the Faith lie broken from the Mander to the Trident; the lords who rose against me kneel in the ashes of their own fields, one by one, and press their lips to my ring while their eyes burn with hate.

My uncle told me once, in his way: the dragon rules, and the sheep obey. I did not wish to be my uncle - but they would not let me be anything else. The realm will remember what it cost to rise against Vermithor, and the memory will keep the peace better than love ever did.

There remains only one thing to take from them: the word they denied me, spoken from the ruin of their holiest place.

#bold The realm is broken to the saddle. Now the Faith will say the words. #!

They crown a new High Septon in a borrowed sept, for the old one is ash - and his first act, before septons whose hands shake as they hold the crystal, is to proclaim the Doctrine of Exceptionalism a holy tenet of the Faith of the Seven. My grandsire won his crown with dragons and kept it with mercy. My uncle had the dragons and not the mercy. And I? I offered the realm wisdom, and it chose to teach me that only the fire is ever truly heard.

#bold The doctrine stands - written not in ink, nor in blood, but in fire. #!

Proclaim a grand tournament!

#bold The Dragonpit is open. The tournament begins. #!

Rickard Redwyne does not forget. He rides as if the din of the Dragonpit is only wind, taking each tilt cleanly, lowering his lance at the proper breath, and sending better-born boys tumbling before him. By the final pass even the hardened knights are nodding to one another.

The joust belongs to Ser Simon Dondarrion of Blackhaven.

Alysanne forbids Jonquil Darke and Tom the Strummer from joining them, though neither takes the command kindly. I cannot fault her. This is sport only by courtesy. From the royal gallery it looks very much like war.

I answer with peace, precedent, and the dangers that gather around a woman's crown. Every reason sounds colder spoken aloud to the woman who helped me build this realm. If a woman is of less use to me than a man, she says, then I can have no further need of her. Before I can call the words back she has her household making ready for Dragonstone.

Alysanne receives my proclamation without a courtier present to soften it. She asks why [rhaenys.GetFirstName] should lose Aemon's inheritance to [chosen_heir.GetTitledFirstName]. I answer with peace, precedent, and the burdens of rule. Every reason sounds colder spoken aloud to the woman who helped me build this realm. If her counsel and a woman's claim mean so little, she says, then I can have no further need of her. Before I can call the words back she has her household making ready for Dragonstone.

Alysanne receives my proclamation without a courtier present to soften it. She asks how I can answer one death by setting the senior line aside for [chosen_heir.GetTitledFirstName]. I answer with peace, precedent, and the burdens of rule. Every reason sounds colder spoken aloud to the woman who helped me build this realm. If her counsel means so little, she says, then I can have no further need of her. Before I can call the words back she has her household making ready for Dragonstone.
If you must go, then go.
The Elder Line Endures

Alysanne reads the proclamation twice before she looks up. I have named [chosen_heir.GetTitledFirstName], keeping Aemon's place alive through his daughter rather than treating his death as the death of his whole line. My queen does not pretend the lords will swallow it quietly. She only takes my hand and says that today I remembered the law of blood as well as the habits of men.
Whatever resistance comes, we will meet it together.
A Daughter Between Us

I let [maegelle.GetFirstName] speak where pride had kept me silent. She asks me to remember that [alysanne.GetFirstName] and I have survived too much together to let a throne stand between us now. My judgment will stand. My silence need not.
Forgive me, Alysanne.
Alyssa's Last Childbed

Beside [alyssa_daughter.GetFirstName]'s bed, the joy of a newborn son curdles into dread. The bleeding has slowed, but a burning sickness has taken hold of her, and the maesters lower their eyes when I demand certainty. A septa kneels at the foot of the bed and prays to the Mother for mercy, and I have never in my life wanted so badly to believe she is heard. My laughing, fearless daughter reaches for my hand and asks me, twice, whether the boy is well.
I am not leaving this room.
Baelon is shattered by Alyssa's death. He becomes #V Widowed#! and will honor her memory by never marrying again.
Alyssa's Son

Little [infant_aegon.GetFirstName] fights for every shallow breath. The wet nurse tells me he has his father's hands. The maester tells me nothing at all. In the hour of the wolf, when the oldest die and the youngest are born, the tiny fingers close once around mine and then fall still.
The Stranger is gentle with the very small. I will hold to that tonight.
The Match Before Us

[alyssa_daughter.GetFirstName] followed [baelon.GetFirstName] from the day she could walk. For years he complained that his sister trailed him about like a puppy and had the poor judgment to be born a girl. She was six when a wooden sword came round in the training yard and broke her nose; it healed crooked, and she has never once asked a maester to trouble himself over it.

Somewhere between then and now the complaining stopped.

[alysanne.GetFirstName] settled the matter long ago and has never pretended otherwise. When other names were set beside our daughter’s, my queen answered that the girl was meant for [baelon.GetFirstName], and would hear nothing further about it.
