Betroth Alyssa to Baelon.
Their marriages are mine to arrange, and not yet.
Alyssa and Baelon remain unbetrothed and may receive other proposals. Alyssa will not face her last childbed unless she weds Baelon and bears his son.
A Stitch in Baelon's Side

[baelon.GetFirstName] comes back from the hunt complaining of a stitch in his side. By the hour of the bat he cannot stand. The pain settles deep in his belly, fever follows it, and every hour takes more out of him. I summon the Grand Maester and tell him to try everything the Citadel taught him, and then whatever it did not.
Spare nothing. Not one draught, not one hour.
A burst belly

Five dawns have come and gone beside [baelon.GetFirstName]'s bed. The maesters' draughts dull the pain but cannot touch whatever is killing him beneath it. My son wakes long enough to know me, squeezes my hand, and says that he is tired. I tell him to sleep, then. I sit through the sixth dawn alone.
The Stranger has taken my son.
The Fever Breaks

I scarcely trust the Grand Maester when he tells me the swelling has eased. Then [baelon.GetFirstName] drinks without retching, sleeps without fever, and wakes demanding to know how long I mean to keep him abed. The recovery is slow. Every step of it gives me back a son I had already begun to bury.
Reward every hand that tended him.
Maegelle's Vocation

Every night [maegelle.GetFirstName] reads from the #italic Seven-Pointed Star#! before she sleeps. She is gentle where some of her sisters are fierce, quiet where the court demands display, and happiest when a septa lets her tend a sick child or copy out a page of doctrine. Alysanne reminds me of the promise she made the Mother at this daughter's birth: one girl given to the Faith in thanks. I expected tears when we put it to her. Maegelle asks when she may begin.
Then Oldtown has her, and the Seven a servant better than I deserve.
My daughter stays at court.
The Prince Who Preferred Books

Neither sword nor horse nor dragon has ever held [vaegon.GetFirstName]'s attention for long. Books do. The Grand Maester tells me plainly that my son wants the patience for ravens and the warmth for a castle, but that the Citadel might yet make an archmaester of him if numbers and higher mysteries are allowed to take his life. I tell Vaegon that a ship sails for Oldtown within the fortnight. For once I almost see him smile. “Yes, Father,” he says. “Good.”
Send Vaegon to the Citadel.
A Prince of the Blood will not be a servant.
A Husband for Daella

When I ask [daella.GetFirstName] what she remembers of the Vale and of [eyrie_lord.GetTitledFirstName]'s court, she speaks warmly of its courtesy, and warmest of all about [rodrik.GetTitledFirstName]'s kindness to her. Gentleness will matter more to this daughter than splendor. I could also leave her hand unpromised a while longer and look for another man worth her trust.

When I ask [daella.GetFirstName] what she remembers of the Eyrie, she speaks warmly of its courtesy, and warmest of all about [rodrik.GetTitledFirstName]'s kindness to her. Gentleness will matter more to this daughter than splendor. I could also leave her hand unpromised a while longer and look for another man worth her trust.

When I ask [daella.GetFirstName] what she remembers of the Eyrie, her answer is all courtesy and no hope. The Arryn boy once spoken of for her is beyond reach now, by death or by another man's contract. Gentleness will matter more to this daughter than splendor, and I would sooner keep her waiting than hand her to the wrong house.
Then it will be [rodrik.GetTitledFirstName]. She will have kindness, at least.
No promises yet. There may be a better man for her.
Daella remains unbetrothed and may receive another marriage proposal.
The Eyrie's Empty Place

Grave news comes down from the Eyrie. [eyrie_lady.GetTitledFirstName] has taken suddenly ill, and the Vale's maesters hold little hope of her. I cannot welcome a death that clears Daella's road. I can only notice that the road has opened.
The Vale buries her first. My daughter’s name can wait on their grief.
A flight to the Eyrie

[alysanne.GetFirstName] is climbing onto Silverwing before [daella.GetFirstName]'s letter has left my hand. Our daughter is with child and frightened, and my queen will not have the width of the realm between them for it. I tell myself the Eyrie's maesters are skilled. Alysanne does not argue. She only looks at me the way she looked at me when I dismissed the first warning about this match.
Fly fast. I will send word ahead to the Eyrie.
A Daughter for a Daughter

One mercy and one cruelty come in the same raven. [daella.GetFirstName] has borne a healthy girl, and the labor has left her burning with a fever the maesters cannot reach. She is not alone. I am the width of a kingdom away, and the raven was days in coming. In the sept below they are already lighting candles to the Mother, which is what men do when the maesters have stopped promising.
I forced too much, too soon. Forgive me, sweet girl.
A Bride for White Harbor

Alysanne proposes [white_harbor_lord.GetTitledFirstName] for [viserra.GetFirstName]. The lord of White Harbor is older than our daughter and has been married before, but he is canny, courteous, and master of the greatest port in the North. Viserra hears only age and distance. If her mother admires the man so greatly, she says, her mother is welcome to marry him herself. Beneath the insult sits another ambition. Viserra has been watching the Iron Throne for years, and an unwed brother would keep her close to it.

Alysanne's White Harbor match for [viserra.GetFirstName] has come to nothing. The lord she chose is dead, or else pledged elsewhere. Viserra takes the failure for a victory and turns her eyes back toward the Iron Throne. If a brother of hers is still unwed, the old customs of our blood offer one road. Otherwise her hand stays unpromised until I find something better.
Approve the match with White Harbor.
I betroth Viserra to Aegon.
I betroth Viserra to Aemon.
I betroth Viserra to Baelon.
I betroth Viserra to Vaegon.
I betroth Viserra to Gaemon.
I betroth Viserra to Valerion.
Find Viserra a better match than White Harbor.
No royal betrothal is made. Viserra remains free to receive another proposal.
One Last Night

On the eve of her departure [viserra.GetFirstName] begs one last night among the friends of her girlhood, and I allow it. The rest I have from the gold cloaks and from companions too frightened to lie well: inn after inn, wine and laughter and all the freedom she was certain White Harbor would take from her, then a race home through the dark in the hour of the owl. A mare came down in the Street of Flour. They carry her to me before dawn with her neck broken, and she cannot hear a word I say.
My daughter... no.
Carried Home

The hammering on the door comes in the hour of the wolf, and it is [bedchamber_witness.GetFirstName] of the Kingsguard who brings her, white cloak spoiled to the elbow and my daughter senseless in his arms. [alysanne.GetFirstName] is out of the bed before I am.

[bedchamber_witness.GetFirstName] tells it to me as the companions told it to him, and no two of them told it alike: inn after inn, a race home through the dark, a mare down in the Street of Flour. By every reckoning [viserra.GetFirstName] should have gone into the stones head-first. She did not. Whether her hands remembered what the wine had drowned, or the Mother was minding a girl who had not thought to ask her, I will never be told plainly. Two ribs are broken and there is wine still sour on her.

When the maester has gone she opens her eyes, sees the pair of us standing over her, and has the gall to smile.

The Seven kept you when I could not. I will not spend that gift shouting.
The Princess's Companions

[saera.GetFirstName] has gathered five young courtiers around her. [braxton.GetFirstName] Beesbury, whom the court already calls the Stinger for his tongue, is handsome, proud, and dangerously pleased with himself. [jonah.GetFirstName] Mooton and red-haired [roy.GetFirstName] Connington are heirs with more courage than caution. [alys_turnberry.GetFirstName] Turnberry and [perianne.GetFirstName] Moore match my daughter in age, in beauty, and in appetite for mischief. They feast and hawk and hunt and sail as one company. I see harmless youth in their laughter, and also the beginning of a court inside my court.
Under my roof, where I can see them. Better that than Flea Bottom.
This is not proper company for a princess.
Tom Turnip at the Blue Pearl

The fool Tom Turnip is found at a pleasure house called the Blue Pearl, so drunk he can scarcely stand. [braxton.GetFirstName], [jonah.GetFirstName], and [roy.GetFirstName] are there beside him, laughing at whatever humiliation carried a royal fool into such a place. The servants say this is no single night's folly. For more than a year Saera's companions have been trading rooms and gifts and secrets beneath my own roof. I have let the rumors pass because I wanted them to be nothing. They are not nothing.
Confine the men. Alysanne and I will learn the truth.
Three Girls Questioned

Alysanne questions the girls apart. Perianne Moore weeps. Alys Turnberry confesses that she is with child and cannot say with any certainty which of the young men fathered it. The stories differ in small details and agree in every important one. Saera was not led astray by one seducer. She chose the game, she kept it going, and she made her friends players in it. My queen brings me their answers with her anger held so tightly that her hands shake.
Bring Saera before the Iron Throne.
Like Aegon and Maegor

[saera.GetFirstName] denies nothing. Braxton Beesbury, Jonah Mooton, and Roy Connington have all been her lovers. When I demand to know which man she means to wed, she smiles and offers to take all three, as Aegon the Conqueror took two wives. Then she invokes Maegor as well, and the name empties the hall of sound. I hear my daughter set her appetites beside a conqueror's, and something in me goes very quiet. Across the hall Alysanne's eyes find mine. She is asking me not to say the thing I am about to say.
Confine her. I will judge every culprit.
She is the blood of the dragon. I will hear no more of this.
The Dragonpit Door

Confinement holds [saera.GetFirstName] less than a night. She slips her guards, crosses the city, and is taken at the doors of the Dragonpit. Whether she meant to claim a dragon or only to frighten me, I cannot know. I know what a dragon in her present temper would make of a family disgrace. I have her locked high in a tower under constant guard. The men who shared her sport will face judgment below.
No more evasions. I will pass sentence.
Judgment upon Five

Jonah Mooton accepts marriage to Perianne Moore and the work of making something honorable out of their folly. Roy Connington is offered the Wall or ten years across the narrow sea, and chooses exile. Alys Turnberry will go to a motherhouse until her child is born. Only Braxton Beesbury refuses every mercy. The Stinger demands trial by combat, certain that youth and strength and a morningstar will shame whatever grey champion I put in front of him.
The others have their sentences. Bring Beesbury before me.
This Old Man

Braxton stands before the throne in polished armor, his arrogance untouched by chains. “Then I choose trial by combat. Which of these old men do you mean for me to fight?” I am down the steps before any of my Kingsguard can answer him. Behind him, [saera.GetFirstName] is staring at me as though she has never seen her father before.
This old man. The one whose daughter you seduced and despoiled.
Blackfyre and the Morningstar

We meet in full armor with our shields up. He carries a morningstar and all the strength of nineteen years. I carry Blackfyre and the patience of a man who has outlived a war, a rebellion, and most of the people he began with. He comes at me the moment the herald steps back, hammering iron against my shield, certain that age must give way if it is struck often enough. I give ground. I let him spend pride as though it were strength. Then I begin to press forward.
Then the Warrior judges between us.
The Stinger's Last Breath

His blows slow. The shield sags, the morningstar drags at his arm, and when he stumbles Blackfyre's point finds the narrow opening of his visor. The yard is silent before the body has finished settling. My daughter does not look away, and neither do I. Afterward I give the order that sends [saera.GetFirstName] to Oldtown, where prayer and discipline may do what my anger cannot.
The Silent Sisters will receive her.
The Old Man Yields

The Stinger's morningstar breaks my guard and puts me down in the dirt. The yard erupts before the Kingsguard can close around us. By the law I invoked myself, Braxton Beesbury has proved his innocence before gods and men. By every face in that yard, he has also wounded the crown. I will not have him murdered for winning a trial I demanded. Saera must still go from this court before her defiance finishes what is left of my family.
Honor the trial. Then Saera goes to Oldtown.
The Motherhouse at Oldtown

[maegelle.GetFirstName] writes from Oldtown. [saera.GetFirstName]'s silks have been taken, her hair shorn, her days divided among prayer, silence, rough cloth, and humble labor. Maegelle does not pretend her sister has embraced any of it. She asks me for patience and promises to instruct Saera herself. My gentle daughter has made peace between Alysanne and me before now.

The motherhouse writes from Oldtown. [saera.GetFirstName]'s silks have been taken, her hair shorn, her days divided among prayer, silence, rough cloth, and humble labor. The septas do not pretend she has embraced any of it. They ask me for patience, and I grant it, though every report says my daughter studies doors and walls more diligently than scripture.
Firm, then. Never cruel. I have seen what cruelty makes of my blood.
A Ship Bound for Lys

After a year and a half the motherhouse finds an empty bed and a novice's robe left folded on it. [saera.GetFirstName] has gone from Oldtown, taken ship, and crossed the narrow sea to Lys, where she now lives under [lys_ruler.GetTitledFirstName]'s peace. She has traded prayer for a pleasure garden and my judgment for her own keeping. I send men to search docks she left weeks ago. It is something to do with my hands.

The Daughter I Will Not Name

Years pass. [saera.GetFirstName] leaves Lys for Volantis, grows rich, and comes to keep a house grander than many lords possess. When someone asks whether I will call her home, I answer that I have no daughter in Volantis. The court is satisfied with that. I am not, and I can still remember fastening her cloak for her when she was too small to manage the clasp.
I will not send for her.
A Letter from Volantis

I know [saera.GetFirstName]'s hand before I break the seal. The letter comes from Volantis, written by a woman who owns her own house and asks me for neither coin nor rescue. She does not excuse what passed between us, and neither do I. She asks one thing only: whether a daughter may cross the sea and speak with her father, without chains or vows or old accusations waiting for her at the quay.
Tell her there will be no chains on the quay.
I cannot reopen that wound.
Gael's Secret

[gael.GetFirstName] keeps out of my sight and away from the household, and has done for a turn of the moon. A traveling singer has left court without taking his leave of anyone, and the servants have begun counting months on their fingers. I have learned what silence can cost this family.
Gently. She is not to be frightened.
The Child Who Never Cried

Grief has hollowed [gael.GetFirstName] out. The singer left her with a child. The child came too early and never cried. There was no name given and no septon called, because to call one would have been to tell the realm. She has carried all of it alone, certain that shame was the only answer she would get if she asked for help. I tell her she is not alone. I cannot tell whether the words reach her.
She is not to be left alone. Not for an hour.
Blackwater Bay

[gael.GetFirstName] is standing where the black water folds around her feet when I reach the shore. She looks back once, not startled, only tired, and walks on. I call her name. I am still calling it when the tide takes her out of sight. The Faith has no gentle word for what she has done. It will not be said over her while I draw breath.
I am too late.
Found Before the Water

I follow [alysanne.GetFirstName] down to the shore and we reach [gael.GetFirstName] before the tide can have her. Our daughter breaks in her mother's arms and speaks at last of the singer, of the lost babe, of the shame that walked her down to the water. We take her home between us.

[gael.GetFirstName] is knee-deep in it when I reach the shore, and the tide does not get her. My daughter breaks in my arms and speaks at last of the singer, of the lost babe, of the shame that walked her down to the water. I carry her back up the strand myself.
Come away from the water, sweetling.
A Crown without an Heir

Baelon is scarcely buried before the petitions reach the Red Keep. One letter argues for the senior branch, another for the nearest living man, a third for age and proven service. Lords who agree on nothing else agree that delay will harden every preference into a faction. I have spent a reign closing the wounds left by disputed crowns. I will not leave a fresh one under my shroud.
Summon Vaegon and hear his counsel.
Send to the Citadel and hear its Seneschal.
Summon [council_maester.GetFirstName] and hear [council_maester.GetHerHis] counsel.
Hear the counsel of the most learned men in Westeros.
The choice is mine. I will name an heir now.
A Harder Answer
The Archmaester's Answer
The Seneschal's Answer
The Grand Maester's Answer
The Maester's Answer

I set the rival claims before him and ask which name will keep the peace. My son refuses to give me one. “Let the lords decide,” he says. Not a council of flatterers in my chamber, but every lord with a claim and every lord sworn to judge it. The realm may accept from its own assembled voice what it would resist from an old king's grief.

The Citadel sends its Seneschal. [council_maester.GetFirstName] comes up from Oldtown with the road still on [council_maester.GetHerHis] robes and spends no more courtesy on a king than the chain requires. [council_maester.GetFirstName] weighs the rival claims a long while and then declines to give me a name at all. “Let the lords decide,” [council_maester.GetSheHe] says. [council_maester.GetFirstName] hears the rival claims out to the end and then declines to give me a name at all. “Let the lords decide,” [council_maester.GetSheHe] says. My councillors lay the rival claims across the table until there is more ink than wood in front of us, and no name among them promises peace. At last one of them offers a harder answer: let every lord with a claim be heard, and let the assembled realm judge among them. The lords may accept from their own gathered voice what they would resist from an old king's grief.
Then I will summon a Great Council.
No. I will not surrender the judgment of my house to lesser lords.
The Road to Harrenhal

I choose Harrenhal, where [harrenhal_lord.GetTitledFirstName] can house more claimants than any living lord should wish to meet at once. Ravens go out from the Red Keep in every direction. For half a year the roads fill with banners, wagons, sworn swords, petitioners, hedge lords, and princely entourages. More than five hundred may sleep within the walls; twice that number will raise tents beneath the black towers. I stay in King's Landing. If the council is to speak freely, it must not mistake my presence for an answer.

The Claims at Harrenhal

Dispatches from Harrenhal arrive in bundles thick enough to bend a maester's back. The claims of [heir_candidate_1.GetTitledFirstName], [heir_candidate_2.GetTitledFirstName], and [heir_candidate_3.GetTitledFirstName] are among those getting a serious hearing, but no two letters agree on what ought to matter most. Lord Baratheon writes that the elder branch cannot be passed over without unmaking every inheritance in the Stormlands. Lord Hightower answers that no woman has ever sat the Iron Throne and none ever should. A Blackwood and a Bracken have found the same side of the question, which unsettles me more than the quarrel did. I stay in King's Landing and read every name that survives them.

The sealed judgments are opened in front of me. Arguments, tallies, warnings, names, and one septon’s letter begging me to remember that the Father judges kings last and hardest. Everything except a law that might have spared me the act itself. Deaths, marriages, vows, and choices made across my whole reign have shaped a family no maester's diagram reduces to a rule. Aemon's death has left more than an empty chair. I have the living members of House Targaryen brought before me one at a time. A pedigree can trace a right through the dead. Only the living can inherit. I mean to look at each of them before I choose.

Two ribs cracked against the cobbles, bound tight by a maester who did not trouble to hide what he thought of the hour she came home at. They will knit. Until they do she cannot draw a full breath without remembering the fall.

This child came into the world ailing and was not expected to keep it. Someone refused to let go.
The Dragon Returns

Word reaches me as I shelter far from court: Maegor is dead. They found my uncle slumped upon the Iron Throne, pale and cold, his own blood pooled beneath him and the barbs of that cruel seat sunk deep into his flesh. Whether the throne claimed him or a hand unseen, no man can say - and few will mourn.

I will not wait for leave. I mount Vermithor, the Bronze Fury, and turn his wings toward King's Landing. The lords and the smallfolk will look up and see a dragon returning - not to burn them, as Maegor did, but to end the terror at last.

I am Jaehaerys of House Targaryen. I mean to take my father's throne and my uncle's ruin and make of them something worthy. My mother shall guide my hand, and Lord Rogar his sword. The work of healing a broken realm begins now.
The Iron Throne is mine.
The Regency

The war for the throne is won before it is truly begun. Most of my uncle's supporters have fled the city; the few who remained, I have taken in chains.

Yet I am a boy of four-and-ten, and a boy cannot rule the Seven Kingdoms alone. So it is agreed. My mother, the Dowager Queen Alyssa Velaryon, shall rule as Queen Regent until I come of age. And Lord Rogar Baratheon of Storm's End - the strong sword who marched to set me upon the throne - I name Lord Protector of the Realm and Hand of the King, to guide my hand in the years to come.

#bold Together, we shall begin to bind the wounds my uncle left. #!
Now the healing begins.
The King's Justice

The realm is full of men who served the Cruel - lords who bent the knee to my uncle, gaolers and confessors who tortured my brother Viserys to death in the black cells, and Maegor's own Kingsguard, white cloaks sworn to a monster.\n\nSome kneel and beg the black. Ser Harrold Langward, once Maegor's Lord Commander, kneels to no one - he denies my right to judge him and demands trial by combat. My mother and Lord Rogar counsel restraint, but the choice is mine alone. How shall the reign of Jaehaerys begin?
Justice, tempered with mercy.

Ser Maladon Moore is executed for his part in the murder of Queen Tyanna. Ser Harrold Langward demands trial by combat; I would take up the sword myself, but the Queen Regent forbids it, and our champion Ser Gyles Morrigen strikes him down. Ser Jon Tollett, Ser Symond Crayne, Ser Olyver Bracken and Ser Raymund Mallery take the black.
Then they all die.
Pardon them all. The realm has bled enough.

Maegor's six are spared the sword and the Wall alike - but mercy is not restoration. Their white cloaks are taken from them, and they are exiled across the narrow sea, to live out their days as hedge knights at the Sealord's court in Braavos. They shall never again stand guard over a king of Westeros.
The King's Peace with the Faith

Word comes from the south: Septon Moon is dead, and the Poor Fellows who besieged Oldtown have melted away like snow. The long war between the dragon and the Seven can end at last - if I will let it.

I will. I swear that the Iron Throne shall protect and defend the Faith of the Seven for all time - but I will not raise the Warrior's Sons and Poor Fellows again, and the Faith Militant shall lay down its swords forever. I lift my uncle Maegor's bounties from the heads of the faithful, and pardon all who repent; in return, the Most Devout acknowledge the King's justice, and the High Septon himself agrees to set the crown upon my head at the Starry Sept. The road to Oldtown lies open.

#bold Men will say I am a king who reconciles, not one who burns. #!
Then let us to Oldtown, and the crown.
A White Cloak for a Warrior's Son

There is one more oath to be sworn. Ser Joffrey Doggett kneels before me - once Grand Captain of the Warrior's Sons, the Red Dog who bore sword and star against my house in the name of the Seven. He is the finest blade the Faith Militant ever raised, and I would far rather have such a man guarding my back than see him hunted through the hills like a beast.

I offer him a white cloak and a place among my Kingsguard. He bows his head, sets aside the star of the Warrior's Sons, and takes the cloak, swearing to shield the king and the royal family with his life.

#bold A former foe of the crown becomes one of its truest swords. #!
Rise, Ser of the Kingsguard.
The Golden Wedding

In this, the nine-and-fortieth year after the Conquest, my mother the Dowager Queen weds Lord Rogar Baratheon in a wedding so lavish the smallfolk are already calling it the Golden Wedding. Storm's End empties its coffers; the feasting will run a fortnight.

I like Lord Rogar well enough, and I respect his strength. Yet he did not think to ask my leave before taking my mother to wife - and I am the King. He names it a love match; I am not so certain. A man who is already my Hand and Lord Protector now weds himself to the Queen as well. I wonder how much of Rogar's heart is truly for my mother, and how much is for the crown that sits so near his hand.

#bold I say nothing. A boy king learns to hold his tongue - and to remember. #!
He might at least have asked my leave.
The War for the White Cloaks

Five white cloaks have hung empty since I cast out my uncle's Kingsguard, and my mother has a notion to fill them: let the finest knights of the realm win their places in a great tourney to follow her wedding. I agree - but I decree the contenders shall fight on foot, not horsed. A foe seldom strikes a king from the saddle.

For seven days they fight, and the jousting is soon forgotten amid wild melees and bloody duels; hundreds of knights vie with axe, spear and sword for the honour of the white. The smallfolk roar themselves hoarse for their favourites - Ser Willam Stafford, Ser Tom the Strummer, a mystery knight who proves to be the woman Jonquil Darke - but when the dust settles, five stand above the rest.

Ser Lorence Roxton, Ser Victor the Valiant, Ser Willam the Wasp, Ser Pate the Woodcock, and old one-eyed Ser Samgood of Sour Hill kneel before me. I bid them rise, sworn brothers of my Kingsguard.

#bold My white cloaks are seven once more. #!
Rise, brothers of the Kingsguard.
A Match for a King

The Golden Wedding done, Lord Rogar turns his ambition to me. A king must have a queen, he says, and my hand is the richest prize in the realm - a bride from Casterly Rock, perhaps, or Highgarden, to bind a great house to the throne. He has candidates already; my mother nods along. And for my sister Alysanne, some lord's heir far away.

They speak of alliances and armies. They do not speak of what Alysanne and I have known since we were children - that we love one another, and mean to wed no one else. I am the blood of the dragon, and the dragon does not bend to a Lord Protector's schemes.

#bold If they will not give us leave, we shall not ask it. #!
We will not be parted.
Flight of the Dragons

We tell no one. In the black before dawn, Alysanne and I steal from the Red Keep to the dragonpit, where Vermithor and Silverwing wait. The Bronze Fury spreads his wings, my sister's she-dragon answers with a cry, and we are gone into the night sky before the regents so much as stir.

Beneath us King's Landing shrinks to a scatter of torches, then the black water of the bay, and then only the wind and the wings and Alysanne laughing beside me. We fly east, toward the ancient seat of our house, where no Hand and no Septon can keep us apart.

#bold To Dragonstone - and to each other. #!
To Dragonstone, and freedom.
A Wedding at Dragonstone

In the ancient sept of Dragonstone, beneath the painted gods and the smoke of a hundred candles, Septon Oswyck weds us. There is no court, no lords, no feast - only my sister's hand in mine, a few loyal witnesses, and the vows themselves.

We are man and wife now, Alysanne and I, king and queen in truth. The High Septon and the Most Devout may gnash their teeth; Lord Rogar may rage until Storm's End trembles. A marriage sworn before the Seven and made whole cannot be unmade.

#bold I take you, Alysanne, and no other, for all the days of my life. #!
Let no one put us asunder.
The Regency's Wrath

The word reaches King's Landing within days, and the storm breaks. Lord Rogar is beside himself - cheated of his schemes, made a fool before the realm, roaring that the marriage must be annulled and the boy king brought to heel. My mother weeps, torn between her son and her new husband.

But rage as they might, the thing is done. I am wed, and soon I shall be a man grown and free of any regent's leash. Yet I am not blind: the Faith will not suffer a brother to bed his sister quietly. When I come into my crown in truth, the Seven will demand their reckoning - and I must be ready to answer it.

#bold The deed is done. Now let the Faith have its say. #!
I am ready for whatever comes.
The Great Council

Balked of the marriage, Lord Rogar plays his last and boldest card. Before the small council he declares that a king who defies his Protector and beds his own sister is no fit king at all - and that the throne should pass to my niece Aerea, daughter of Aegon the Uncrowned, whose line ran senior to mine own. A girl of six, whom Rogar would rule through until she was grown and safely wed to a candidate of his choosing.

For a moment the chamber is silent. Then my mother the Queen Regent rises - and against her own husband, she speaks for me. One by one the council follows her: Lord Rogar's design is refused, and his reach for a puppet-queen dies on the council table.

#bold He has overreached, and the realm has seen it. #!
The council will answer him.
Vermithor will answer him.
The Sixteenth Nameday

On the twentieth day of the ninth moon, in the fiftieth year since my grandsire's Conquest, I turn six-and-ten upon the windswept rock of Dragonstone. I am a man grown now, in the eyes of gods and men alike, and the regency ends as all regencies must. No Protector rules in my name; no Hand schemes to unmake my marriage. Alysanne stands beside me, my queen in truth.

Before I go to claim my throne in earnest, I send five knights of my Kingsguard ahead to King's Landing, to see that all is made ready for the king's return. The Red Keep is to be swept and its gates thrown open. The dragon comes home.

#bold Ready the city. In three days I fly for the capital. #!
Have them make the city ready.
The King Returns to the Red Keep

Three days after my nameday I mount Vermithor and take wing from Dragonstone, and the Bronze Fury bears me over the bay to King's Landing. The smallfolk crowd the streets to cheer as my dragon circles the hill of Aegon and settles in the yard of the Red Keep.

My mother is waiting for me. There has been coldness between us - her marriage to Rogar, his schemes, the crisis over my own wedding - but she is my mother still, and I am her son, and we have both grieved and lost too much to remain estranged. We speak long and privately, and when we are done, the breach between us is healed. Whatever passed between me and her husband, the Dowager Queen Alyssa Velaryon and her king are reconciled.

#bold She is my mother. There will be peace between us. #!
Embrace her.
The Small Council Remade

A king must be served by able men, and my uncle and the regency alike left me a council of the idle, the timid, and the merely fortunate. So I set to work. Some I dismiss outright; some I confirm in their offices, having proven their worth; and to the empty seats I raise men of my own choosing.

Hardest of all to replace is my master of coin, Lord Edwell Celtigar - a man as greedy as he is useless, who understands the counting of his own coppers far better than the treasury of a realm. For a time I despair of finding his equal in incompetence's opposite. In the end I look beyond Westeros entirely, and name a shrewd Pentoshi named Rego Draz to keep the Crown's gold. I fill the lesser offices with my own men, and open the black cells and dungeons of King's Landing, that my uncle's prisoners may see the sun again.

#bold A new council for a new reign. #!
Out with the old, in with the able.
The Lord Protector's Reckoning

One matter remains: Lord Rogar Baratheon. I summon him to the throne room and receive him seated upon the Iron Throne, my council ranged about me, that all might see it is a king who judges him now and no boy. Rogar comes expecting harsh words, perhaps worse - and he is not wrong to fear, for he reached for my crown and would have set a child in my place.

Yet I have not forgotten the other truth: that when Maegor's shadow lay over us all, it was Rogar's strong sword that shielded me and mine, and set me on this throne. So I temper justice with memory. I will pardon him - upon his oath that he shall never again speak a word against me or my queen, and that he shall be an honourable husband to my mother. And his brother Orryn, who on Rogar's word tried to steal the novice Rhaella from her motherhouse to raise a rival against me, I sentence to ten years' exile beyond the narrow sea.

When Rogar, humbled, asks whether the Crown will require hostages of House Baratheon, I say nothing. I only rise, and lead him out to where Vermithor waits - and let the Bronze Fury make my answer for me.

#bold Kneel, my lord, and let this be the end of it. #!
Lord Rogar Baratheon is pardoned upon his oath, and sent home to Storm's End. His brother Orryn is exiled ten years.
The king needs no hostages of House Baratheon - not while Vermithor lives. Lord Rogar takes the meaning well.
I have not forgotten what you did for us. Be at peace.
Hostages? Come, my lord - let me show you Vermithor.
#bold (An Alternate History)#! I will NOT kneel to this boy and his sister-wife.

Before the High Septon

The Starry Sept of Oldtown is the oldest and holiest seat of the Faith in all Westeros, and beneath its great dome of black marble and crystal the light falls in a thousand colours upon the assembled Most Devout. Here, where the Andal kings of old were blessed, I kneel before the High Septon of the Seven.

He anoints me with the seven holy oils - upon my brow for the Father's justice, my eyes for the Crone's wisdom, my hands for the Warrior's strength, and so through all the Seven who are One. I bow my head and swear before gods and men to defend the Faith and rule justly over the realms of men. The old septon's hands tremble as he raises them over me in blessing.

#bold In the sight of the Seven, the anointing is done. #!
I so swear, before the Seven Who Are One.
The First of His Name

The High Septon lifts the crown - and sets it upon my brow. It is done. I rise, no longer a boy king holding a throne by the sufferance of regents, but an anointed sovereign, crowned and blessed before the eyes of the Seven and all the great lords of the realm.

The septon's voice rings out beneath the dome, and the herald takes up the cry, and it echoes from the crystal above:

#bold "All hail Jaehaerys of House Targaryen, the First of His Name, King of the Andals, the Rhoynar, and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms, and Protector of the Realm!" #!

The hall thunders it back at me. The dragon and the Seven are reconciled, and my reign begins not in fire, but in blessing. They will call me the Conciliator.
Long may I reign.
A Novice for the Faith

There is a gentleness owed to the Faith now that the wars are done, and I mean to show it. My niece Rhaella - daughter of my late brother Aegon and my sister Rhaena, and twin to little Aerea - is a solemn, pious child, happier at her prayers than at any dance or feast.

So she is given to the Faith, and sent to a motherhouse at Oldtown to be raised among the septas, to take the white of a novice and one day swear her vows. A princess of House Targaryen serving the Seven: there is no truer sign that the dragon and the Faith are at peace. She goes willingly, and the Most Devout are well pleased.

#bold May the Mother watch over her, and the Crone light her way. #!
She will be raised gently among the septas.
The Storm Refuses to Kneel

So this is how the dragon rewards the sword that saved him. Stripped of the Protectorship, sent home like a scolded boy, made to bend the knee to a stripling who beds his own sister in defiance of gods and men. I marched an army to set this ungrateful whelp upon the Iron Throne - and this is my thanks.

The sword is not yet sheathed. The Faith itself calls their marriage an abomination, and there is another with a better right: Aerea, daughter of Aegon the Uncrowned, of the elder line. A girl, yes - but a girl may be guided, and a realm ruled well through her. And I would not rise alone: the pious Reach, whose lands hold Oldtown and the Starry Sept and the High Septon himself, has no love for a king who weds his sister - the Lord of Highgarden would call his banners to Aerea's cause. Storm's End and the Reach need not kneel to Jaehaerys and Alysanne.

And yet - the boy rides Vermithor, and his sister Silverwing. My brother Orryn is banished, my seat watched, my wife the king's own mother. A wise man knows which storms to ride out.

#bold The storm gathers in my breast. Do I loose it - or swallow it? #!
For Queen Aerea! To war!
No. I swallow my pride, and keep the king's peace.
A Girl Upon the Iron Throne

It is done. The dragon king is fallen, his sister-queen scattered to the winds, and the great hall of the Red Keep echoes with a new cry: Aerea, First of Her Name, Queen of the Seven Kingdoms. She is but a child, sitting small and solemn upon that monstrous chair of melted swords - but the crown is on her brow, and it was my sword that put it there.

The realm is mine to shape now, through her. Or - the thought comes unbidden, gazing at that great black throne - a strong hand might do more than merely guide a queen. But no. She is my queen, and I made her. For now.

#bold The Iron Throne answers to House Baratheon at last. #!
Rule through her. I am the power behind the throne.
#bold (Play as Aerea)#! Take up the girl-queen herself.
The Price of Rebellion

They took Lord Rogar in chains to the foot of the Iron Throne, and there, before the whole court, King Jaehaerys had his head struck from his shoulders. The rebellion is broken. Aerea's cause is ash, her banners burned, and the storm that Rogar raised has blown itself out against the dragon's walls.

The lordship of Storm's End falls to me now, and with it the ruin of his ambition. What is left to House Baratheon is our seat, our pride, and the long memory of how close we came. The dragon reigns, and we endure - as we always have. The dream of a Baratheon-made throne dies upon the block.

#bold The storm is spent. But House Baratheon endures. #!
We endure. There will be other days.
A Wedding at Fair Isle

Word comes from the far west, from Fair Isle in the Sunset Sea. My elder sister Rhaena has known little joy in her life - wed first to our brother Aegon, whom Maegor slew, and then forced into our monstrous uncle's bed as one of his Black Brides. Thrice a queen, and thrice sorrowed. Small wonder she has fled the court and its dragons.

Now she has taken a new husband, on her own terms this time: Androw Farman, second son of the Lord of Fair Isle - a gentle, mild-mannered youth, no warrior and no schemer. It is no great love match, all say, and Rhaena weds him more for the quiet of Fair Isle than for the man himself. But it is her choice, freely made, and after all she has endured she has earned that much.

#bold May my sister find some measure of peace at last. #!
I wish her well, and gladly.
A Hand for the King

The Protectorship is ended and the office of the Hand stands empty. Rogar Baratheon taught me the danger of a Hand who is also the mightiest lord in the realm, with armies and ambitions of his own. This time I will have a Hand who serves the Crown and not himself - a steady man, wise in coin and law and the workings of the realm, whom I can trust as I trust few others.

I find him near to home. Lord Daemon Velaryon of Driftmark, the Lord of the Tides and my mother's kinsman, has served ably as my master of ships. He is no warlord and no schemer, only a capable and loyal man - and that is precisely what I need. I name him Hand of the King, and so begins a partnership that I mean to last the length of my reign.

#bold Rise, Lord Daemon, Hand of the King. #!
Lord Daemon Velaryon, the Lord of the Tides, is raised from Master of Ships to Hand of the King.
The realm is the better for it. Rise, my lord Hand.
The Reforms of Rego Draz

My new master of coin proves his worth at once. Lord Rego - for I have raised the Pentoshi to a lordship, that the Iron Throne need not blush to be served by him - stems the bleeding of the Crown's debts, enough that the great works upon Rhaenys's Hill may resume. But it is not enough to see the Dragonpit finished, and so together we devise a cleverer way to fill the coffers.

We lay a tax upon luxuries and exotic goods - Myrish lace and Volantene silk, Qartheen spices and Lyseni perfumes. It touches no smallfolk, and no honest lord shall feel it; only those who would flaunt their wealth and splendour before the world. And flaunt it they will, Rego assures me, laughing - a vain man will pay any price to be envied. He is right. The coppers become dragons, and the dragons a river of gold.

To this I add a second tax, with a purpose beyond mere coin: henceforth any lord who would raise a new castle, or repair or enlarge an old one, shall pay a heavy toll reckoned by the count of his crenellations. The great lords will think twice before raising their walls higher - and pay the Crown handsomely if they do.

#bold The treasury swells, and the Dragonpit shall be finished after all. #!
A shrewd design, my lord. Proclaim it.
The Second Wedding

Half a year after I came at last to King's Landing, Alysanne departs Dragonstone to join me, and a moon's turn later we are wed a second time - not in secret as before, but openly, before the Iron Throne and the eyes of the realm. There can be no whispering now that the King and Queen are not truly married.

The rites are performed by a septon new-come to my service: Barth, a smith's son of humble birth and boundless mind, the most learned man I have ever met. I mark him well; I think he shall rise far. The ceremony itself is a modest thing - the treasury is bare, and barely a thousand guests attend, a poor show beside the splendour of Rogar and my mother's Golden Wedding. Yet I would not trade it for a thousand golden weddings.

Alysanne is my sister, my queen, and my truest friend in all the world; there is no one living who knows my heart as she does, nor I hers. That night, as man and wife before gods and men at last, we lie together.

#bold Whatever storms may come, we shall face them as one. #!
My queen. My sister. My soulmate.
A Septon for a Hand

Lord Daemon Velaryon has served the crown long and faithfully, but the Lord of the Tides grows old, and the tides call him home. The realm expects me to reach for a great lord to take up the chain - a Tully, a Tyrell, an Arryn, some proud name with proud banners.

The realm will be disappointed. There is one man at this court who has read every book in the Red Keep's library and written better ones; who argued the Doctrine with septons and the harbor accounts with Rego Draz, and bested both; who fears neither gods, nor lords, nor telling his king that his king is wrong. He is the son of a blacksmith. He wears a septon's robes. And he has the finest mind I have ever met.

The great lords may gnash their teeth. Wisdom does not wear a house's colors.

#bold Septon Barth shall be my Hand. The realm will laugh - and then, for forty years, it will marvel. #!

The Handship stands empty, and the realm expects me to reach for a great lord to fill it - a Tully, a Tyrell, an Arryn, some proud name with proud banners.

The realm will be disappointed. There is one man at this court who has read every book in the Red Keep's library and written better ones; who argued the Doctrine with septons and the harbor accounts with Rego Draz, and bested both; who fears neither gods, nor lords, nor telling his king that his king is wrong. He is the son of a blacksmith. He wears a septon's robes. And he has the finest mind I have ever met.

The great lords may gnash their teeth. Wisdom does not wear a house's colors.

#bold Septon Barth shall be my Hand. The realm will laugh - and then, for forty years, it will marvel. #!
The chain goes to the finest mind in the realm.
Lord Daemon Velaryon steps down with honor, and #bold Septon Barth#! - the blacksmith's son who kept the Red Keep's library - becomes Hand of the King.
The Dragon's Child

Baelon has begun to chase every shadow shaped like wings. He is still small, but he is dragon's blood, and fear taught too late can curdle into something worse.

The Dragonpit stands ready. Balerion sleeps within its dark. I should show my son what our house has kept, and what it must never take lightly.

#bold A prince of the blood must meet what makes his House great. #!
Bring him to the pit.
Baelon the Brave

I had meant only to let Baelon look.

Balerion lies before us like a hill of black iron, smoke leaking between teeth longer than my son's arm. Before I can catch him, Baelon darts forward laughing and strikes the Black Dread upon the snout.

For one heartbeat, the world holds still. Then Balerion opens a molten eye, and Baelon laughs harder.

A white cloak lets out the breath the rest of us had forgotten to take. "That boy is brave," he says, "or mad."

#bold By nightfall the whole Red Keep has chosen the kinder word. #!

Alysanne's half-year of warmth has gone before me and made the way smoother than it might have been: the hall is correct, the feast is laid, the words are all the proper words. But the eyes that watch me down the length of that smoky hall belong to lords whose fathers knelt to mine under threat of fire, and none of them have forgotten it.

Winterfell will be won the way Alysanne won it, or not at all: slowly.
Then let us see what the North would show its king.
The Crypt of Winterfell

We go down with torches, past the stone kings in their rows — the Kings of Winter with their swords across their knees and their direwolves at their feet, ten thousand years of them staring blind into the dark. Lord Alaric says nothing the whole descent.

He stops at a tomb newer than the rest, the stone still pale. The likeness is of a big man with a blade across his knees, and I do not need the name read to me.

'My brother Walton,' Alaric says. 'He took Ice north against the men Your Grace sent to the Wall, and beheaded the first of them with it. The others he chased beyond the Wall, into the haunted forest. The giants tore him into five pieces. We buried what came back.' He raises the torch, and his eyes come to mine at last. 'You spared those knights, Your Grace. I have wondered these eight years what it is a king says to that.'
Your brother paid my share of that mercy. I am sorry, Lord Stark.
(Say nothing. The dead ask for nothing.)
Two Wolves at Table

There is no tomb to visit, and no grudge kept above one. Instead there is a feast — and at the high table, a Lord of Winterfell telling his bannermen, once more and by popular demand, the tale of the winter the King came north.\n\n'Rimegate was to be MY grave, like as not,' Walton Stark says, with the grim satisfaction the North reserves for its narrowest escapes. 'Storming a Wall castle in a mutiny winter — ask the Watch what that costs. And then the sky rattled, and the mutineers' gate opened, and the whole cursed business was done before my column cleared the Gift.' He raises his cup to me, and the hall comes up with him. 'To the debt the King paid HIMSELF, sers. The North remembers good as well as ill.'

There is no tomb to visit and no grudge in this hall — only a feast, and a Lord of Winterfell who unbends over the course of it from granite to mere oak.

It is late, and the fires low, when Walton Stark speaks of it at last. 'My father used to say your justice bought this peace, Your Grace. Maegor's knights, the ones you gave the sword.' He turns his cup slowly. 'Men called it harsh in the south, I am told. No northman called it so. Oathbreakers sent to the Wall are oathbreakers still — the Watch has buried brothers for lesser mercies. You spent six heads to spare it that. Winterfell counts the bargain cheap.'

Alysanne catches my eye down the table. LISTEN, her look says. The North is telling you it trusts you.

There is no tomb to visit and no old wound under this hall — only a feast in the northern manner, which is to say: enormous, unhurried and honest.

The Lord of Winterfell drinks with me, speaks of harvests and wolf packs and the state of the kingsroad, and somewhere past midnight — the precise moment is hard to fix — I understand that I have stopped being inspected and started being hosted. Alysanne's half-year of groundwork, spent in a single evening.

The North gives nothing quickly. What it gives, it means.
To Winterfell, then. And to patient queens.
The New Gift

She ambushes me at Winterfell, exactly as promised, and she does it before the assembled court, which is how I know she means to win.

'The Night's Watch holds a hundred leagues of Wall on a beggar's portion,' my Queen says. 'Nine hundred men, where ten thousand once stood, feeding themselves off Brandon's Gift while the lords south of it grow fat facing the wrong way. I ask the King to double the Watch's lands: every league of it south of the Gift, from the one sea to the other. Let it be called the New Gift, and let the Wall eat.'

The hall has gone very quiet. The lords whose lands those are stand along it like standing stones. Lord Stark's face is shut. The Lord Commander's men, down-table, have stopped breathing.
It shall be done. The New Gift, to the Watch, in perpetuity.
The canon grant: the counties of the New Gift pass to the Lord Commander of the Night's Watch. The Watch will not forget it — and the northern lords will not forget it either.
The Wall has land enough. The North keeps its own.
Queenscrown

In the new-given lands there is a village on a lake, with a stone towerhouse on a holm reached by a hidden causeway, and it is there the Queen's progress shelters on its last northern night.

The village women feast her on what they have. In the morning, as the column forms up, Alysanne unpins the golden circlet from her hair — the one she has worn the length of this progress — and sets it in the hands of the village elder, to be kept by the place forever in memory of a queen's stay.

They are calling the village Queenscrown before the column is out of sight. They will be calling it that, I suspect, when everyone who could say why is ten centuries dust.
The North will keep that crown longer than any vault of mine.
The Road Home

South again — wings and sails and the long column unwinding down the kingsroad, out of the snows and into autumn country where the air stops hurting.

King's Landing smells of smoke and salt and too many people, which is to say: of home. The city gives its King and Queen a roaring welcome; the court gives us a mountain of petitions; and Alysanne, who charmed Winterfell and feasted with black brothers and set her dragon at the edge of the world, looks down at the Red Keep from Silverwing's back, she tells me, with something like disappointment that it is over.

It is not quite over. There is a thing she heard in the North that she has been waiting the whole road home to lay before me.
Then let us hear it. All of it.
The First Night

She comes to me not as my wife but as a petitioner, and she brings her women's courts with her — every hall from White Harbor to Mole's Town, every voice that spoke when the lords were sent out of the room.

'The right of the first night,' Alysanne says. 'The lord's claim to a bride before her husband. The maesters call it old custom and the lords call it seldom used, and I have sat with the women it was used upon. In the North, in the riverlands — everywhere, my love. It is not custom. It is a cruelty with a pedigree. No law of gods or men should suffer it, and you are the law of men.'

She sets no scroll before me. She only waits. She told me at Winterfell she knew what I would do when I had heard what she had heard.
Then hear the law of men: the first night is ABOLISHED, everywhere.
The canon reform: Queen Alysanne's women's courts end the right of the first night throughout the Seven Kingdoms.
The great northern lords who kept the old right will resent it — a small, lasting grievance against both the King and the Queen.
The lords' old rights are the lords' affair. I will not reach into their halls.
Together

The magisters of Pentos and Tyrosh are sent home with fair words, no treaty and identical expressions of silk-wrapped outrage, and I find I can live with that.

The retinue is already at sea. The court is scandalized twice over — once that the Iron Throne declined the honour of mediating, and once more that the King and Queen mean to make the whole progress side by side, two dragons over one column, like some tale out of the Conquest.

Alysanne is entirely unrepentant. 'They will forgive you a lost treaty,' she says, pulling on her riding gloves. 'The North would never have forgiven us a lost progress.'
Two dragons north, then. The realm will look up.
The kingsroad, together — a true royal progress, every league of it.
Wings North Together

Vermithor and Silverwing take the kingsroad's line north wingtip to wingtip, bronze and silver against the winter sky, and below us the realm comes out of doors to watch its King and Queen pass over.

The Neck crawls beneath like a drowned world; then the North opens, white and endless, and Alysanne's laughter carries across the gap between our dragons in scraps whenever the wind allows. She has wanted this for ten years: the two of us, the cold clean air, the world made small.

Grey towers on the horizon. Winterfell rising. Let us see what the North makes of two dragons come courting.
Down, now. Courtesy waits in that cold yard.
The Kingsroad

The column makes its leagues in the old way, and I begin to understand what I have been missing from dragonback all these years.

A king on a dragon is an omen; a king on the road is a MAN, and the smallfolk come out to see the difference. They line the hedgerows with their children on their shoulders. They bring petitions, ale, complaints about the local septon, one goat (a gift; we kept it). At every halt the tent of petitions fills, and I do more small justice in a week of mud than in a month of throne room.

The baggage train, for once, is exactly where I am.
On, north.
The Neck

The causeway through the Neck is a spear-haft of dry ground laid across a green-brown drowned world, and the column walks it two abreast with the bog breathing on either side.

The crannogmen do not show themselves, and show themselves constantly: a reed screen that was not there an hour ago, a child's woven charm hung at the road's edge, once a spear standing upright in the mud a long bowshot out — planted, the guides say, as a courtesy. Greywater Watch is somewhere out there, moving, as it always is.

The men do not love this road. I find I do. No army has ever forced it, and no dragon is needed to hold it: the Neck holds itself.
And past it, the North.

The Lord of Air

Lord Rego Draz is dead in the mud of Flea Bottom, and I am told there was not enough left of his head to close his eyes.

He was being carried from the Red Keep to his manse on the Street of Silk, in that gilded palanquin this city has laughed at for ten years. In the heart of Flea Bottom a crowd closed around him. A dozen men, hungry, half in drink, and full of the same talk that has run through my streets since the cold came - that bread costs three times what it did, that the Shivers came ashore off a ship, and that the man who counts the king's coin is a Pentoshi. His bearers set him down and ran.

One of them worked a cobblestone loose from the street I paved and brought it down on him again and again until the work was done.

I made Rego a lord because the magisters of Pentos would not have him, low-born and rich as he was. He had no land, no castle, no sworn sword; my own court named him the Lord of Air for it, and he laughed louder at that jest than any man in the hall. He filled my treasury for eleven years and never once lied to me about a figure. He was murdered a quarter mile from my gates for having been born across the narrow sea.

The gold cloaks seal the poorest quarter of King's Landing street by street. The city will give up its names, and hate the king for the asking.
It was the winter that killed him, not men. Leave it.
No hunt is called. The murderers of the king's own master of coin walk free, and every lord in the realm will mark what the king's peace is worth.

They have the alley roped off, for whatever that is worth. The palanquin is still lying on its side where it fell, the gilt scraped down to the bare wood by people helping themselves. The stone was found four steps from him, and it is not a small stone.

No one saw anything. That is the answer at every door on that street, and at every door on the three streets behind it. Flea Bottom has lived under the King's Peace for eleven years and has learned precisely how much of itself it may keep back from me.

A dozen men, in a city of forty thousand, in a winter, in the dark. My council tells me the smallfolk will close over this like water over a dropped coin, and that a king is wiser to mourn than to hunt.

#bold My council has forgotten who paid to pave that street. #!
Then I will walk it myself, and Vermithor will wait above the rooftops.
The king goes down into Flea Bottom in person, with a dragon's shadow crossing the roofs behind him. Terror will pry the names loose faster than any search. #bold Very likely to find the killers.#!
Gold cloaks. Every hovel, every cellar, door by door.
The City Watch searches the quarter house by house. Slower, cruder, and the city will remember the boots on its stairs. #bold An even chance of finding the killers.#!
A dragon of gold for a name. Flea Bottom has never yet refused coin.
The crown buys informers in the poorest quarter of the city. Flea Bottom will sell its own. #bold Likely to find the killers.#!
The King's Justice

It took two days once I walked in myself.

A king in Flea Bottom is a strange animal, and a king in Flea Bottom with a bronze dragon turning slow circles over the rooftops is a thing that loosens tongues no coin could. By the second evening I had eleven names, and by the third night I had eleven men.

I think I wanted monsters. What is kneeling in the yard beneath the Red Keep is a fishmonger, two dyer's apprentices, a man who buried three children this winter, and seven more cut from the same cloth. Thin. Filthy. More frightened of me than Rogar Baratheon ever was in the whole of his life.

The one who lifted the stone will not stop saying that he has a wife. He has said it perhaps forty times. He has not once said that he is sorry, and I do not believe he understands, even now, that he has done a thing a man could be sorry for.

Alysanne asks what good their deaths will do a man already dead. Rego would have asked me the price. But I have held a peace over this city for eleven years, and a peace that will not answer murder is only a word.

#bold Whatever I do in that yard tomorrow, the whole realm will learn it by heart. #!

It cost me less than a good horse.

Open them from throat to groin, and hang what is left from my walls.
The killers are disembowelled and their bodies hung from the walls of the Red Keep, where the city cannot look away from them. King's Landing will be a very quiet city for a very long time.
Hang them. It is a death, and a death is enough.
Eleven men hang at the gallows in the ordinary way. The city takes the lesson, though not so deeply as it might have.
The Wall. Men who cursed the cold can go and live in it.
The killers take the black. The Night's Watch is given eleven men who will not enjoy the north, and the Faith is given a king who did not spill blood he could have spared.
The hand that held the stone will hang. The rest go home as hungry as they came.
One man dies. Ten walk out of the yard alive, and tell every soul in Flea Bottom what the king did. The lords of the realm will call it weakness.
A Cold Trail

Nothing. Not one name.

Eleven or twelve men beat a lord to death in a public street in the middle of the afternoon, in a quarter where four thousand people live stacked on top of one another, and there is not a witness in all of King's Landing. Doors that were open are shut. Men who were drinking in the Street of Flour that day were, it turns out, all of them at their mothers' bedsides.

The commander of my gold cloaks stands in front of me and tells me that Flea Bottom protects its own, and that this is not defiance so much as a habit older than my house. He is right, and I would very much like to strike him for it.

Rego Draz sailed across the narrow sea because I asked him to. He served eleven years and made this crown solvent for the first time since my grandsire took it. And I cannot give him the one thing a king is supposed to be able to give anyone.

#bold I have paved these streets, walled this city and fed it through a winter, and it will not give me eleven names. #!
Flea Bottom keeps its own. So be it. Call off the search.
The hunt ends with nothing. The lords of the realm will note that a man may murder the king's master of coin in the king's own capital and grow old.
Then all Flea Bottom answers for it. Fines, whippings, and the Watch.
The whole quarter is punished for what a dozen men did. No justice is done, but no one in King's Landing will mistake the king for a soft man.
The Sons of Rego Draz

Three young men are waiting in my audience chamber, and every one of them has his father's nose.

Gessio is nineteen and has had the ledgers open for four days already; he can tell me to the copper what the crown owes and to whom, without notes. Illyrio is seventeen and cannot make himself look at me. Myrio is fifteen and is weeping, and is trying very hard to do it without moving his face.

All three are baseborn, got on women Rego never married and never pretended to have married, and all three are the only heirs he troubled to acknowledge. Behind them stands the manse on the Street of Silk, the warehouses along the river, four ships, the debts of half the lords of the Reach, and a fortune that my master of laws describes, carefully, as an embarrassment.

None of it is bound to them. A lord with no lands leaves nothing his king may not simply take, and there is not a septon in this city who would trouble to call it theft.

#bold Rego Draz crossed the narrow sea because Pentos would not have him. Today I decide what Westeros gives him back. #!
Every coin of it goes home to Pentos with them. My own ships will carry it.

The Draz fortune leaves Westeros whole, in the hands of Rego's sons. They will build houses of their own on it in Pentos - and every free city will hear how the Dragon treats a foreigner who served him faithfully.
Gessio stays. His father's head for figures did not die in that alley.
Gessio Draz is taken into the king's court. The rest of his father's wealth sails for Pentos with his brothers.
He left no lawful heirs. Count every coin of it into my treasury.
The crown takes everything Rego Draz owned. The gold is real and it is needed - and so is the reputation the crown is spending to get it.
The Empty Seat

The small council meets with a gap in it that no one will look at directly.

A name has already been put forward, and it is a good name, which is what a Hand is for. Ser Martyn Tyrell of Highgarden: heir to nothing in particular, pleasant, well-liked, married these three years to Florence of House Fossoway. No lord in the Reach could take offence at him, and lords taking offence is a thing I have had a bellyful of this winter.

He is also, and I say this having now spoken with him twice, not a clever man.

Rego could hold four ledgers in his head and lie to me about none of them. Whoever sits in that chair inherits a treasury that has just paid for a plague, a famine and a winter, and inherits it in the middle of all three.

#bold The chair is only a chair. What matters is who does the counting. #!
Ser Martyn, then. The Reach will be pleased, and the Reach is worth pleasing.
Ser Martyn Tyrell is named master of coin. He is agreeable, he is safe, and he cannot add.
Gessio Draz. He has held those ledgers well since his father died.

Rego's bastard son takes his father's seat at nineteen. He is the ablest man in the room by a wide margin, and every lord in the realm will be told that the Dragon has given the treasury to a foreign whore's son.
No one. I will count it myself until I find a man who can.
The king keeps the treasury in his own hands. It will be well kept, and it will cost him every hour he does not have.
The Lady Who Counts

It has taken me the better part of a year to work out why the accounts stopped being wrong.

Ser Martyn brings them to me himself every moon's turn, and answers well enough at first, and badly the moment I go past the second page. Last week I went past the second page. He went red, and glanced at the door, and said he would have the figure by evening. He had it by evening. It was correct to the copper.

His lady wife does the counting. She has done all of it since the day he sat down. Florence of House Fossoway, taught her letters and her sums by an uncle who had no sons and no fixed notion of what a daughter is for, has been running the treasury of the Seven Kingdoms for a year out of a solar in the Tower of the Hand, while her husband carries her arithmetic downstairs and puts his name to the bottom of it.

Alysanne has known for at least six moons. Alysanne did not think it worth troubling me with.

#bold The realm's coin is in excellent hands. They are simply not the hands the realm believes. #!
It works. Leave the ledgers be, and Ser Martyn his dignity.
Nothing is said aloud. Ser Martyn remains master of coin in name, and grows a great deal better at the office, for reasons the court is content not to examine.
Then let her have the chair, and the name that goes with it.
Lady Florence Fossoway is named master of coin openly, the first woman ever to sit that seat. She will be very good at it. The lords of the Seven Kingdoms will be very loud about it.
A master of coin who cannot count is no master of coin. Both of them, out.
Ser Martyn is dismissed and his wife with him. House Tyrell and House Fossoway will both remember the humiliation.
Flea Bottom Under Steel
Gold cloaks stand at every mouth of every alley. The city obeys, and the city remembers.
The King's Justice Remembered
What was done to Lord Rego's killers was done where the whole city could see it. King's Landing has not forgotten, and does not intend to.
The Hungry King's Mercy
The king was murdered of a friend and answered with bread. The smallfolk of King's Landing will speak of it for a generation.
The Draz Fortune Seized
The crown took a foreign lord's wealth the week he was buried. Every merchant from Braavos to Volantis heard of it, and the ships put in elsewhere.
The King's Own Physicians
The master of coin is a stout man past his best years, and the crown cannot spare him. The maesters of the Red Keep attend him whether he wishes it or not.
His Lady Does the Counting
Ser Martyn carries the ledgers down from the solar and puts his name to them. His wife wrote every figure in them.

The Queen in the East

My sister Rhaena comes to me now that the wedding feasts are done - twice a queen, twice widowed, hounded from refuge to refuge through all of Maegor's reign. Of the three heads of my father's line, hers has borne the heaviest crown of griefs, and she asks now for the only thing she has ever asked of me: a place that is hers, where no one may ever again bid her come or go.

There is only one seat worthy of her: Dragonstone, the ancient citadel of our house, where Aegon dreamed his conquest and the dragons nest in the smoking mountain. She will rule it in her own right, with her own court about her and Dreamfyre in the yards. The realm will call her the Queen in the East, and the realm will not be wrong.

#bold The eldest line takes the eldest seat. It is her due, and long past owed. #!
Dragonstone is yours, sweet sister. No one shall move you again.
The Sun Chaser

Dreamfyre's wings darken the courtyard of the Red Keep, and my sister storms from the saddle in a fury I have not seen since Maegor lived. Lady Elissa Farman - her dearest friend, mistress of Dragonstone's ships, sister to her own husband - is gone. Fled in the night, west then east, and with her three dragon eggs out of the hatcheries beneath the Dragonmont.

Rhaena begged me keep it quiet, and quiet it must be kept: if the realm learns that dragon eggs can be plucked from Dragonstone like apples from an orchard, every thief and every foreign prince will dream the same dream. But quiet is not the same as idle. Elissa sold her jewels in Pentos, and men who describe her all mention the same thing: she means to build a ship, the like of which no one has seen, and sail beyond the maps.

The eggs will not sail with her. Eggs are heavy, and gold is heavier still. She will sell them - and there is one buyer rich enough, close enough, and hungry enough.

#bold Follow the gold. All gold flows to Braavos. #!
Quiet ships and quiet coin. Find where she has taken them.
Pretty Stones

The answer comes back across the narrow sea wrapped in silk and insolence. The Sealord of Braavos regrets that he knows nothing of any stolen eggs; and even if he possessed such curiosities, he observes, unhatched dragon eggs are nothing more than #italic 'pretty stones'#!. In the same breath - the same letter, all but the same sentence - the Iron Bank announces that, as a token of its high regard for the Iron Throne, it is prepared to forgive the greater part of the crown's debts.

So that is the price of three dragons: my debts, and my silence. Rego Draz calls it the finest bargain the crown will ever be offered. Perhaps he is right. But let the Sealord hear this much, and hear it plainly: eggs are stone until they are not.

#bold If ever those eggs hatch, the Sealord's Palace will be the first thing to burn. #!
The Iron Bank forgives the greater part of the crown's debts - #bold 1000 gold#! - and the matter is buried. The three eggs remain in the Sealord's vaults... unhatched. For now.
Take the bargain. But they have been warned.

The Eggs Come Home

The Titan of Braavos watched my fleets pass beneath its legs, and the lagoon burned. The Sealord who called the eggs of Dragonstone 'pretty stones' has learned what stone becomes in dragonfire; his successor was pleased to discover the three eggs in the palace vaults after all, and more pleased still to hand them over.

Three eggs - one black as midnight, one green as summer, one cream and gold - ride home to Westeros in a chest of iron, under guard no thief alive could pass. Whatever sleeps within them will sleep beneath the Dragonmont, where it belongs, or hatch in a Targaryen cradle.

#bold What was taken from the dragon has been taken back. Every vault across the narrow sea will take note. #!
What was stolen from dragons, dragons reclaim.
The Titan Holds

Braavos does not kneel. The lagoon city has no fields to burn and no castles to break - only water, stone, mist and money, and all four defeated me. My fleets came home fewer than they sailed, the Iron Bank has called in every debt with interest, and the Sealord keeps his 'pretty stones' with a courtesy more wounding than any taunt.

The realm whispers that the Old King reached across the sea and came back with an empty hand. The whispers are true. The eggs sleep in Braavos still, and I must live with the knowing.

#bold Some wars are lost in fog and ledgers. But eggs are stone until they are not - and Braavos should still remember it. #!
The sea has beaten better men. But the warning stands.
Deaths on Dragonstone

Grim word from my sister's island seat, and it comes sealed thrice over. Death has crept through Dragonstone like a fog: old Maester Culiper, dead at his letters. Then, one after another, the ladies of Rhaena's own court - Cassella Staunton, Septa Maryam, Alayne Royce, and last Samantha Stokeworth, who fought it for a day and a night, screaming. Rhaena has barred her own gates, and begs to know what curse has come to her hall.

It is no curse.
